modules.summary: The clock is read in minutes, a day is split into a.m. and p.m., hours are changed into minutes and days into hours, how long something takes is worked out, a date is written in two ways, and a calendar and the leap year are read.

media.title: Days That Move and Days That Stay
media.context: Opens the chapter, played once before anything is read or written.
media.description: A ninety second animated opener, played once before anything is read or written. A wall calendar page for one year hangs on a plain wall, and a small oil lamp appears on one day in the autumn, glowing, with a full moon beside it in the sky above the calendar. The page flips to the next year and the lamp appears again, but on a different day of the month, with the moon again at its fullest, so the lamp's day has plainly moved. The page flips once more and the lamp lands on yet another day. The scene then changes to a birthday card standing on a table beside a small cake with candles. A calendar page behind it shows the card's day ringed in vermilion, and as the pages flip year after year the ringed day stays on the very same place, so this day has plainly stayed. Finally a plain card appears with three empty boxes in a row, and a small hand-drawn question mark floats over them. Nothing is counted aloud, nothing is said and no word is written.
media.teaching_notes: Play it once before anything is opened. Ask only two things: which day moved from year to year and which day stayed, and what the three empty boxes at the end might be for.
media.generation_prompt: Animated chapter opener, 90 seconds, 16:9, flat picture-book style, no narration, no on-screen words and no music. A cream wall carries a large wall calendar page for one year, a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first. A small brass oil lamp appears on one day of an autumn month on the page and glows, and a round full moon shines in the sky painted above the calendar. The page flips like a leaf to the next year's page; the lamp appears again, glowing, on a different day of the month, with the full moon again at its fullest, and the first lamp's place stays empty. The page flips again and the lamp lands on a third day. Cut to a wooden table with a small birthday card standing on it beside a little cake with two candles, and behind them the calendar page with one day ringed in vermilion. Pages flip year after year, and in every page the ringed day sits in exactly the same place of the same month. Cut to a plain white card on the table with three empty rounded boxes in a row, and a small question mark rises over them. Every step is slow and unhurried, and each result is held still for a moment so it can be seen. No captions, no words, no narration, no music, no people and no faces.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch once. Say which day moved and which day stayed. Say what you think the three boxes are for.

topics.detailed_summary: The chapter opens on a box about festival days. Some festivals follow the moon, so their dates change from year to year, one in October one year and in November the next. Festivals counted by the calendar the whole world uses stay on the same date every year, one on the twenty-fifth of one month and one on the thirty-first of another. The box then asks a question and leaves it with the child: how do you write the dates for events like school assignments or birthdays? The Recap Exercise under it asks the child to fill six blanks with clock words, hour, minute, noon, midnight, night and morning, and to write the time shown on six school clocks, and the next topic takes that exercise up. A line on page 125 sends the child back to this box once the child can write and read a date. The opener asks and leaves it. It has no tool, no objective and no activity.
important_points: Some festival days fall on a different date each year and some on the same date.
A date says the day, the month and the year.
We need a way to write a date so that everyone reads it the same.
The page asks how to write dates and does not answer yet.
There is no new method on this page and no objective on this topic.

media.title: The Hands and the Minutes
media.context: Plays first in this topic, on its own watch concept, before the tool. It explains the whole topic in four short parts, one for each concept, and ends by sending the child to the tool.
media.description: A narrated, animated explainer of about 115 seconds, in the chapter's flat picture-book style, spoken in plain words with short sentences. A wall clock showing ten forty has a short vermilion hand and a long deep blue hand. The short hand is the hour hand and tells the hours, and the long hand is the minute hand and tells the minutes. A digital clock shows the same time with a colon between the hours and the minutes. The minute hand is counted in fives from one number to the next until it stops on the eight at forty minutes, and twelve fives fill a whole round, which is one hour. It ends by sending the child to the Read the Clock tool.
media.teaching_notes: Play it once before the tool is opened. Afterwards ask three things: which hand is short and what it tells, which hand is long and what it tells, and how many minutes pass when the minute hand moves from one number to the next. Have a paper plate clock with two paper hands to hand. The tool brings its own new times, so nothing in the video is a question from it.

Scenes in order, each with the exact narration to speak: Scene 1. Picture: A cream ground. A round wall clock with a near-black rim and the numbers 1 to 12 in near-black hangs in the middle. It has a short vermilion hand and a long deep blue hand, neither with an arrowhead, set to 10:40: the minute hand points at the 8 (240 degrees) and the hour hand points almost at the 11 (320 degrees). A small question mark floats over each hand. To the right stands a digital clock showing 10:40 in plain digits. Narration: Look at this clock. It has two hands. One hand is short and one hand is long. Which hand tells the hours? Which hand tells the minutes? Let us find out. Scene 2. Picture: The short vermilion hand pulses once and takes the label Hour hand with a small vermilion tag Hours. The long deep blue hand pulses once and takes the label Minute hand with a small deep blue tag Minutes. A thin near-black arc follows the hour hand from the 10 up to where it stands, just before the 11, and the number 10 lights in vermilion beside the clock. Narration: The short hand is the hour hand. It tells the hours. The long hand is the minute hand. It tells the minutes. The hour hand has passed the ten and has not reached the eleven. The hour is ten. Scene 3. Picture: The digital clock grows beside the wall clock. Its 10 is vermilion, the colon is near-black and its 40 is deep blue. A line joins the 10 to the hour hand and a line joins the 40 to the minute hand. The two clocks sit side by side, both reading 10:40. Narration: A digital clock shows the same time with figures. The hours come first. Then come two small dots called a colon. Then come the minutes. This one shows ten, then forty. Both clocks tell the same time. Scene 4. Picture: The clock is set to 10:00 with the deep blue minute hand straight up at the 12. The hand steps to the 1 (30 degrees), then the 2 (60 degrees), and so on, and at each number a small deep blue number appears outside the rim: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40. The hand stops on the 8 (240 degrees) and the label 40 minutes lights. The vermilion hour hand creeps from the 10 to 320 degrees as the minute hand steps. Narration: How many minutes pass from one number to the next? Count along with me. From the twelve to the one is five minutes. Five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five, forty. The minute hand has stopped on the eight. That is forty minutes. Scene 5. Picture: The minute hand carries on from the 8 to the 12, filling the rest of a ring of twelve deep blue five-minute tiles round the dial. Beside the dial: 12 x 5 = 60 in deep blue. The clock now reads 11:00 and the vermilion hour hand stands on the 11 (330 degrees). A green label under the dial reads 1 hour. Narration: How many numbers are on the clock? There are twelve. Twelve fives make sixty. The minute hand takes one hour to go all the way round. Then the hour hand has moved on to the next number. Scene 6. Picture: The clock set to 10:40 appears again with its digital twin. The hour hand is ringed once in vermilion and the minute hand is ringed once in deep blue. The words Read the Clock appear at the end. Narration: Let us remember. The short hand tells the hours. The long hand tells the minutes. From one number to the next is five minutes. Next, watch how to say the time, and then open Read the Clock. The last line of the video names the tool, the Read the Clock, and the video ends there.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch and listen to the whole video. Then say which hand is the hour hand and which hand is the minute hand.

It ends by sending the child to the Read the Clock tool.

Scenes in order, each with the exact narration to speak: Scene 1. Picture: A cream ground. Two wall clocks stand side by side. The left one reads 1:25 (minute hand at the 5, 150 degrees, hour hand just past the 1, 42.5 degrees) and the right one reads 8:40 (minute hand at the 8, 240 degrees, hour hand just before the 9, 260 degrees). Over the left clock float the words past and ?, over the right clock to and ?. Narration: People say the time in different ways. When do we say past? When do we say to? Let us find out. Scene 2. Picture: The 1:25 clock grows alone. The right half of its dial, from the 12 to the 6, is tinted pale deep blue with the label Past. A deep blue arc follows the minute hand from the 12 clockwise to the 5 with small numbers 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 along it. The hour hand stands just past the 1 (42.5 degrees). A digital clock reads 1:25 and a caption reads 25 minutes past 1. Narration: Look at the right side of the clock. When the minute hand is here, we say past. Count from the twelve to the minute hand. Five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five. It is twenty-five minutes past one. Scene 3. Picture: The 8:40 clock grows alone. The left half of its dial, from the 6 to the 12, is tinted pale deep blue with the label To. A deep blue arc runs from the minute hand on the 8 up to the 12 with small numbers 5, 10, 15, 20 along it. The hour hand stands almost on the 9 (260 degrees). Beside the clock: 60 - 40 = 20 in deep blue. A caption reads 20 minutes to 9 and a digital clock reads 8:40. Narration: Look at the left side of the clock. Here we say to. Count the minutes still left to reach the next hour. From the eight to the twelve: five, ten, fifteen, twenty. The hour hand is almost at the nine. We say twenty minutes to nine. Sixty minus forty is twenty. Scene 4. Picture: A clock reads 4:30: the minute hand points straight down at the 6 (180 degrees) and the hour hand stands half way between the 4 and the 5 (135 degrees). A deep blue half-circle of the dial is filled in and labelled half past, with 30 minutes written on it. The clock slides aside and a second clock reads 11:15: the minute hand points at the 3 (90 degrees) and the hour hand stands just past the 11 (337.5 degrees). A deep blue quarter of the dial is filled in and labelled quarter past, with 15 minutes written on it. Narration: The minute hand points straight down at the six. That is half way round the clock. Half of sixty is thirty minutes. We say half past four. At the three, the minute hand is a quarter of the way round. A quarter of sixty is fifteen minutes. We say quarter past eleven. Scene 5. Picture: A clock reads 5:45: the minute hand points at the 9 (270 degrees) and the hour hand stands almost on the 6 (172.5 degrees). A deep blue arc from the 9 to the 12 is filled in and labelled quarter to, with 15 minutes written on it. A caption reads quarter to 6, and a digital clock reads 5:45. Narration: The minute hand is on the nine. It is on the left side. We count the minutes to the next hour. Fifteen minutes are left before the hour hand reaches the six. We say quarter to six. Look at the hour hand. It is almost at the six. Scene 6. Picture: A single bare dial appears with the 3, 6 and 9 ringed in deep blue and labelled quarter past, half past and quarter to, and a right-side and a left-side tint labelled past and to. The words Read the Clock appear at the end. Narration: Let us remember. On the right side we say past. On the left side we say to. The six means half past. The three means quarter past. The nine means quarter to. Next, open Read the Clock. Read the time and set the hands. The last line of the video names the tool, the Read the Clock, and the video ends there.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch and listen to the whole video. Then say how you would read a clock when the minute hand is on the right side and when it is on the left side.

media.title: Read the Clock
media.context: Grade 3, the first working topic of the time chapter. An adult sees a clock being read, which a paper plate clock does well. What is being settled is which hand does which job, that a number on the face can be an hour or a number of five minute steps, and that the side of the clock the long hand is on decides whether we say minutes past or minutes to. A child who reads the number the long hand points to as the hour will say the time wrongly with great confidence, and a child who counts the long hand's number as minutes will say that a hand on the 4 is 4 minutes.

Two hands, two jobs. Which hand tells the hour?
Move the minute hand one number at a time. Count in fives.
Which side is the long hand on? Say minutes past or minutes to.
Look at the long hand. Is it at the three, the six or the nine? Say the time.

Free play. Turn the hands and say the time as you like.

Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the long hand again. Count the minutes in fives from the twelve.
voice.onNext: A new clock. Which hand will you read first?
voice.opening: A wall clock and a digital clock, both waiting for the hands to move.
voice.onFinish: You said every time by counting the minutes.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Turn the hands and say the time as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Two hands: the hour hand and the minute hand
Five minutes from one number to the next
Minutes past and minutes to the hour
Half past, quarter past and quarter to

placement.where: After each child has made a paper plate clock with two card hands and set a few times on it by hand, and before any time is written on the board. The tool is what lets both hands turn together while the digital clock follows, and what shows the hour hand creeping on as the minute hand goes round, which a paper clock turned by hand does not make easy to see.

answer_key.rule: A clock has two hands. The short hand is the hour hand and tells the hour. The long hand is the minute hand and tells the minutes. The minute hand takes 5 minutes to move from one number to the next, so counting in fives from the 12 gives the minutes past the hour. One round of the minute hand is 60 minutes, which is one hour. On the right side of the clock we say minutes past the hour. On the left side we count the minutes to the next hour. The minute hand on the 6 is half past, on the 3 it is quarter past, and on the 9 it is quarter to the next hour.
answer_key.wrong: The clock is shown again with its minutes written round the edge and the minute hand walked from the 12 to its number in fives, each step lit in turn, and the past and to tint shows which side it is on. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The short hand is the hour hand. It tells the hour.
The long hand is the minute hand. It tells the minutes.
The short hand points to the 2 and the long hand is on the 12, so it is 2 o'clock.
items.answer: The short hand is the hour hand. It is 2 o'clock.
items.question: The wall clock in the school library has its short hand pointing to the 2 and its long hand pointing to the 12. Which hand is the hour hand, and what hour is it?
items.checkpoint: The short hand is the hour hand and the long hand is the minute hand.
items.misconception: Calling the long hand the hour hand because it looks like the bigger hand.

steps: The minute hand takes 5 minutes to move from one number to the next.
From the 5 to the 6 is 5 minutes, from the 6 to the 7 is 5 more, and from the 7 to the 8 is 5 more.
Three moves of 5 minutes give 15 minutes.
items.question: The clock above the school bell has its minute hand on the 5. A little later the minute hand is on the 8. How many minutes have passed?
items.checkpoint: Each move from one number to the next is 5 minutes, so count in fives.
items.misconception: Saying 3 minutes, because the hand moved past 3 numbers.

steps: The long hand is on the right side of the clock, so we say minutes past the hour.
Count in fives from the 12: the 1 is 5 and the 2 is 10.
The short hand is just past the 4, so the hour is 4.
It is 10 minutes past 4, or 4:10.
items.question: At football practice the clock on the pavilion wall has its long hand on the 2 and its short hand just past the 4. How many minutes past the hour is it, and what time is that?
items.checkpoint: On the right side say minutes past the hour, and count in fives from the 12.
items.misconception: Saying 2 minutes past 4, because the long hand is on the 2.

steps: The long hand on the 6 is halfway round the clock.
Halfway round is half past the hour.
The short hand has passed the 2 and not reached the 3, so the hour is 2.
It is half past 2, or 2:30.
items.question: The kitchen clock has its long hand on the 6 and its short hand halfway between the 2 and the 3. What time is it? Say it with half past.
items.checkpoint: The minute hand on the 6 means half past.
items.misconception: Saying half past 3, because the short hand is near the 3.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: The digital alarm clock in the bedroom shows 5:20. Which number is the hour, and which is the minutes?
items.final_answer: The 5 is the hour and the 20 is the minutes

items.question: A kitchen clock has its minute hand on the 7. Count in fives from the 12. How many minutes past the hour is that?
items.final_answer: 35 minutes, counting 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35

items.question: The clock at the railway station has its long hand on the 8. Is the long hand on the left or the right side, and how many minutes is it to the next hour?
items.final_answer: The left side. It is 20 minutes to the next hour, because the 8 is 40 minutes past

items.question: A watch shows the long hand on the 3. Do we say quarter past or quarter to?
items.final_answer: Quarter past, because the long hand on the 3 is on the right and a quarter of the way round

items.question: At the bus stop a child says the long hand of the clock is the hour hand because it is longer. Is the child right? Which hand tells the hour?
items.final_answer: No. The long hand is the minute hand. The short hand is the hour hand and it tells the hour

items.question: The school bell rings when the long hand of the hall clock points to the 10 and the short hand is between the 2 and the 3. Say the time two ways.
items.final_answer: 10 minutes to 3, or 2:50

items.question: The alarm clock in the bedroom must ring at quarter to 5. Where does the minute hand point, and what is the time in numbers?
items.final_answer: The minute hand points to the 9. The time is 4:45

items.question: A clock in the school hall runs without stopping from midnight to noon. How many rounds does the minute hand make, and how many does the hour hand make?
items.final_answer: The minute hand makes 12 rounds and the hour hand makes 1 round, because from midnight to noon is 12 hours

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

writes 5, 10 and so on round the outer edge of the face

says the time aloud and in writing

media.teaching_notes: Give each child a paper plate clock with two card hands of different lengths before the tool opens, and ask them to set a few times and say them aloud. Always ask which hand is meant before a number is read, and count the minutes in fives from the 12 with a finger. Wait for a child to say which side of the clock the long hand is on, rather than saying it for them. Say half past, quarter past and quarter to every time the long hand is on the 6, the 3 or the 9. topics.summary: The short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes, five minutes from one number to the next, and a time is read as minutes past or to the hour.

content.text: Watch the video and listen closely. Which hand tells the hours, which hand tells the minutes, and how many minutes pass from one number to the next? The short hand is the hour hand and it tells the hours. The long hand is the minute hand and it tells the minutes. From one number to the next, the minute hand moves 5 minutes. topics.detailed_summary: The Recap Exercise asks the child to write the time on six school clocks, for prayer, maths class, a short break, English class, music class and the end of school. The page then names the two hands of a clock. The hour hand is short, tells the hours passed and goes round once in twelve hours. The minute hand is long, tells the minutes passed and goes round once in an hour. A digital clock shows the hours and minutes in digits with a colon between them. The minute hand takes five minutes to move from one number to the next, and twelve numbers of five minutes make sixty minutes for one round, so the minutes are written on the outer edge of the clock face. Six clocks show different ways of saying a time: twenty-five minutes past five, half past eight, five minutes to four, quarter past eight, quarter to ten and five minutes past four. When the minute hand is on the right of the clock we say minutes past the hour, and when it is on the left we say minutes to the next hour. An example sends a child to market at four o'clock and back after the minute hand has made three rounds, so at seven o'clock. A Critical Thinking box asks how many rounds each hand makes in a day. Exercise 10.1 writes three clocks as minutes past and minutes to, and draws the minute hand for four times.
important_points: The short hand is the hour hand. The long hand is the minute hand.
The minute hand takes 5 minutes to move from one number to the next.
One round of the minute hand is 60 minutes, which is 1 hour.
On the right of the clock we say minutes past. On the left we say minutes to the next hour.
Half past, quarter past and quarter to are the three special times to say.

media.title: A Whole Day: A.M. and P.M.
media.context: Plays first in this topic, on its own watch concept, before the tool. It explains the whole topic in four short parts, one for each concept, and ends by sending the child to the tool.
media.description: A narrated, animated explainer of about 129 seconds, in the chapter's flat picture-book style, spoken in plain words with short sentences. The same clock face shows ten to seven in the morning and ten to seven in the evening, so we need a way to tell them apart. The hour hand goes round the clock twice in a day, twelve hours and twelve hours, so a day has twenty-four hours. The middle of the day is noon and the middle of the night is midnight. The morning half of the day strip is a.m. and the other half is p.m., and a time is written with the label after it, six fifty a.m. and two forty p.m., while noon and midnight take neither label. It ends by sending the child to the Morning or Night tool.
media.teaching_notes: Play it once before the tool is opened. Afterwards ask four things: how many times the hour hand goes round in a day, what we call the twelve o'clock of the day and of the night, which half of the day is a.m. and which is p.m., and where noon and midnight take a label. Have a paper clock and a strip of paper cut for a day to hand. The tool brings its own new times, so nothing in the video is a question from it.

One calm, friendly English voice speaks at a slow, even pace, and leaves a two second silence after every question before the answer. The words are written for the ear: short sentences, plain words, every number said in words. Show on screen what the voice is saying, as it says it. On-screen text is only labels, numerals and symbols, and never a copy of the narration. No brand names, no faces, no cartoon characters, no music. Picture rules for this chapter: Flat, friendly primary-school picture-book illustration of REAL everyday things that tell or mark time, each one recognisable at a glance and drawn in its own natural colours: a wall clock, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a brass school bell, a stopwatch, a wall calendar page, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a birthday card. Clean vector shapes, even fills, a single consistent line weight, no gradients, no drop shadows, no texture. Every clock is exact: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand six degrees a minute, the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute. Neither hand has an arrowhead and the two hands never lie on top of each other where the child is to read them. The clock face, rim and numbers are near-black #2B2B2B on cream. A time is written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone. Noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m. A length of time is a bar laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end. A bar that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces, and the two pieces are added. Colour code, used consistently in every frame of this chapter. The hour hand and the hours are vermilion #D55E00. The minute hand and the minutes are deep blue #0072B2. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue #56B4E9. The p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber #E69F00. The time reached, a length of time worked out and the answer are green #009E73. Real objects keep their natural colours, and the ground is #FFFDF7. A date is written in boxes, a day box, a month box and a year box. A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, with the first day of the month in the right column. Countable things are at most thirty to a frame, drawn large enough to count at a glance, separated and never overlapping one another. Empty space is better than a crowded picture. Scenes in order, each with the exact narration to speak: Scene 1. Picture: A cream ground. A wall clock in the middle reads 6:50: the minute hand points at the 10 (300 degrees) and the hour hand stands just before the 7 (205 degrees). To its left is a flat picture of a school building under a pale sky with a low sun just rising, and to its right a flat picture of the same school under a darkening sky with a street lamp lit and a crescent moon. A question mark floats between the two pictures. Narration: This clock shows ten to seven. It is ten to seven in the morning. It is also ten to seven in the evening. How do we tell them apart? Let us find out. Scene 2. Picture: A long day strip runs left to right under the clock. The hour hand sweeps once round while a vermilion bar fills the left half of the strip with the label 12 hours, then sweeps a second time while a vermilion bar fills the right half with the label 12 hours. Under the strip: 12 + 12 = 24 hours in green, and the label A day, 24 hours. Narration: Watch the hour hand go round the clock. One round is twelve hours. It goes round a second time. Twelve hours and twelve hours make twenty-four hours. A day has twenty-four hours. Scene 3. Picture: The day strip fills the screen. In the middle of the strip a high round sun shines, with a digital face under it reading 12:00 and the label 12 noon. At the left end and at the right end of the strip a crescent moon hangs over a street lamp, each with a digital face reading 12:00 and the label 12 midnight. No clock hands are drawn. Narration: Look at the middle of the day strip. The sun is high in the sky. That is twelve o'clock in the day. We call it noon. Look at the two ends of the strip. The moon is out. That is twelve o'clock at night. We call it midnight. Scene 4. Picture: The left half of the day strip, from the left midnight to noon, is tinted sky blue with a sky blue tag a.m.; the right half, from noon to the right midnight, is tinted amber with an amber tag p.m. Three flat picture cards drop onto the strip one by one: a sunrise with the time 6:50 lands in the sky blue half and takes a sky blue a.m. tag; a school bell with the time 2:40 lands in the amber half, past the sun, and takes an amber p.m. tag; a lit lamp under a moon with the time 9:05 lands in the amber half, near the right end, and takes an amber p.m. tag. Narration: The day strip has two halves. The morning half is a.m. The other half is p.m. Where does ten to seven in the morning go? It goes in the a.m. half. Where does two forty in the afternoon go? It goes in the p.m. half. Five past nine at night is in the p.m. half too. Scene 5. Picture: A school notice card writes the time 6:50 with a sky blue a.m. tag after it, and a second card writes 2:40 with an amber p.m. tag after it. At the right, the two labels 12 noon and 12 midnight each stand beside an empty tag with a near-black cross on it, to show that no a.m. or p.m. is written. The cards line up in a tidy row. Narration: To write a time, put a.m. or p.m. after it. Ten to seven in the morning is six fifty a.m. Two forty in the afternoon is two forty p.m. What about noon and midnight? They take neither a.m. nor p.m. We write twelve noon and twelve midnight. Scene 6. Picture: The whole day strip appears with its sky blue half and its amber half, the sun in the middle and the moons at the ends, and the three cards 6:50 a.m., 2:40 p.m. and 9:05 p.m. sitting on their halves. The words Morning or Night appear at the end. Narration: Let us remember. A day has twenty-four hours. Noon and midnight are the two twelve o'clocks. The morning half is a.m. and the other half is p.m. Next, open Morning or Night. Sort the times and write them. The last line of the video names the tool, the Morning or Night, and the video ends there.

media.title: Morning or Night
media.context: Grade 3, the second working topic of the time chapter. An adult sees a rule being learnt, a.m. before noon and p.m. after it, which a printed pair of clocks states. What is being settled is that one clock face shows two different times of a day, that a day has twenty-four hours because the hour hand goes round twice, and that the twelve of the day and the twelve of the night have names of their own. A child who reads a small number as a.m. will call five in the evening a.m., and a child who writes 12 with p.m. has not yet seen that noon stands alone.

source_tool.description: A long day strip fills the width of the working area, from midnight at the left to midnight at the right with noon in the middle. Its left half, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and labelled a.m., and its right half, from noon to midnight, is amber and labelled p.m. A sunrise over a school is painted at the left, a high sun at noon in the middle, and a moon over a street lamp at both ends. A wall clock hangs above the strip with a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand, and a Sun slider moves a sun along the strip while the hands turn with it, the hour hand sweeping twice round from one end to the other. Picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football, a dinner plate and a bed can be dragged onto the strip. A time card takes a time from the number pad and a label from the a.m. and p.m. buttons, and a Noon and midnight button writes the words noon and midnight, which take no label. A green Answer tag holds what the child has written. A Plain clock button redraws the clock as a bare dial. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many times have been placed.
source_tool.art_direction: A school day from sunrise to lamp light / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at where the sun is. Is it before noon or after noon?
voice.onNext: A new time. Find which half of the day it is in.
voice.opening: A whole day on one strip, with a sun and a moon.
voice.onFinish: You put every time on the right half of the day.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Slide the sun and place the times as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A day has twenty-four hours
Noon and midnight
a.m. and p.m.

placement.where: After each child has marked noon in the middle of a long paper strip, coloured the morning half sky blue and the evening half amber, and stuck picture cards of the day on it by hand. The tool is what sweeps the hour hand twice round while the sun crosses, and what puts a time and its label side by side, which a paper strip cannot do on its own.

answer_key.rule: A day has 24 hours, because the hour hand goes round the clock twice and 12 plus 12 is 24. 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight. The time from midnight to noon is a.m. The time from noon to midnight is p.m. A time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, but noon and midnight take neither.
answer_key.wrong: The day strip is shown again with the sun carried along it from midnight, the morning half lit sky blue and the evening half lit amber, and the time is dropped on the half it falls in. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Once round the clock is 12 hours.
Going round twice is 12 plus 12.
12 plus 12 gives 24, so 24 hours pass. That is one whole day.
items.answer: 24 hours, which is one whole day
items.question: The hour hand of the wall clock in the school hall goes once round the clock in 12 hours. How many hours pass while it goes round twice?
items.checkpoint: The hour hand goes round the clock twice in a day, so a day has 24 hours.
items.misconception: Saying 12 hours, because the clock face only shows 12 numbers.

steps: Both hands point to the 12, so it is 12 o'clock.
The sun is high in the sky, so it is the day.
12 o'clock in the day is noon.
items.answer: 12 noon, because the sun is high in the day
items.question: In the school kitchen the cook sees both hands of the wall clock pointing straight up to the 12 while the sun is high in the sky. Is it 12 noon or 12 midnight?
items.checkpoint: 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight.
items.misconception: Saying midnight because both hands point to the 12, without looking at the sun.

steps: Noon is the middle of the day.
From noon to midnight is p.m.
The evening is after noon, so 5:40 in the evening is 5:40 p.m.
items.question: The street lamp outside the school switches on at 5:40 in the evening. Is that a.m. or p.m.?
items.checkpoint: From midnight to noon is a.m. From noon to midnight is p.m.
items.misconception: Choosing a.m. because 5:40 looks like a small number.

steps: 6:55 in the morning is after midnight and before noon.
From midnight to noon is a.m.
So the time is written 6:55 a.m.
items.question: The alarm clock wakes a child for the school bus at 6:55 in the morning. Write the time with a.m. or p.m.
items.checkpoint: A time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it.
items.misconception: Leaving off a.m., so nobody can tell whether it is the morning or the evening.

items.question: The hour hand of the kitchen wall clock goes once round in 12 hours. How many times does it go round in a whole day?
items.final_answer: 2 times. A whole day has 24 hours

items.question: The moon shines over the street lamp and both hands of the clock point to the 12. Is this time called noon or midnight?
items.final_answer: Midnight, because it is 12 o'clock at night

items.question: Football practice starts at 3:45 in the afternoon. Is that a.m. or p.m.?
items.final_answer: p.m., because the afternoon is after noon. It is 3:45 p.m.

items.question: The class goes to the library at 9:25 in the morning. Write the time with a.m. or p.m.
A train leaves the station at one midnight and arrives at the next midnight. How many times does the hour hand of the station clock go round, and how many hours is that?
items.final_answer: Twice, and that is 24 hours

items.question: At noon the school lunch bell rings. A child writes noon as 12 and then adds p.m. What should be written instead?
items.final_answer: 12 noon. Noon takes no a.m. or p.m.

items.question: On a school day the sun rises at 6:20 in the morning, lunch is at 12:40 in the afternoon, football practice is at 4:50 in the afternoon and the child goes to bed at 10:15 at night. Which of these times are a.m. and which are p.m.?
items.final_answer: 6:20 is a.m. The times 12:40, 4:50 and 10:15 are p.m.

items.question: Write each time with a.m. or p.m., or write noon or midnight: the lamp at the school gate switches off at sunrise at 5:35 in the morning, the cook starts lunch at 11:45 before noon, the lunch bell rings at 12 o'clock in the day, and the night guard starts at 12 o'clock at night.
items.final_answer: 5:35 a.m., 11:45 a.m., 12 noon and 12 midnight

media.teaching_notes: Give each child a long paper strip before the tool opens. Ask them to mark noon in the middle, colour the morning half sky blue and the evening half amber, and stick picture cards of their own day on it, writing each time with a.m. or p.m. Ask which things happen before noon and which after, and wait for a child to say why noon and midnight take no label rather than saying it for them. If a child calls a small number a.m., ask whether the sun is up before or after noon. Use fresh times: the printed clocks and sentences are the child's to read and write.
media.generation_prompt: Build a day tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A long day strip fills the width of the working area, from midnight at the left to midnight at the right with noon in the middle. Its left half is sky blue and labelled a.m., and its right half is amber and labelled p.m. A sunrise over a school is painted at the left, a high sun at noon, and a moon over a street lamp at both ends. A wall clock hangs above the strip with a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand, drawn exactly, and a Sun slider moves a sun along the strip while the hands turn with it, the hour hand going twice round. Picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football, a dinner plate and a bed are dragged onto the strip. A time card takes a time from the number pad and a label from an a.m. button and a p.m. button, and a Noon and midnight button writes the words, which take no label. A green Answer tag holds what the child has written. A Plain clock button redraws the clock as a bare dial. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of times placed. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. media.title: Noon and Midnight
media.context: Shown on the second concept of the third topic, where 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight.
media.description: Two rectangular panels sit side by side. The left panel shows a daytime scene with a light blue sky and green grass, featuring a two-storey red-brick building with four windows and a brown door, and a bright yellow sun with eight rays overhead. Below it is printed "12 noon: the sun is high" and "a.m. ends, p.m. begins". The right panel shows a night scene with a dark blue sky and ground, featuring a pale circular moon, seven yellow stars, and a glowing street lamp. Below it is printed "12 midnight: it is dark" and "p.m. ends, a.m. begins".

topics.summary: A day has 24 hours, the hour hand goes round twice, and a time is written a.m. from midnight to noon and p.m. from noon to midnight.

content.text: Watch the video and listen closely. How many hours are in a day, what are noon and midnight, and how do a.m. and p.m. tell the two halves apart? A day has 24 hours, because the hour hand goes round the clock twice. The 12 o'clock of the day is noon, and the 12 o'clock of the night is midnight. The hours after midnight and before noon are a.m. The hours after noon and before midnight are p.m.
content.publication_text: A day has 24 hours, because the hour hand goes round the clock twice. The 12 o'clock of the day is noon, and the 12 o'clock of the night is midnight. The hours after midnight and before noon are a.m. The hours after noon and before midnight are p.m.

concepts.concept_name: Watch and listen: a day, noon, midnight, a.m. and p.m.

content.text: The hour hand goes round the clock once in 12 hours. How many times does it go round in a whole day? Twice. 12 plus 12 is 24. So a day has 24 hours.
content.publication_text: Twice. 12 plus 12 is 24. So a day has 24 hours.

topics.detailed_summary: A man has to catch a flight at seven o'clock, but is it seven in the morning or seven in the evening? Two clocks show the same seven o'clock and are labelled morning and evening. A day has twenty-four hours, twelve o'clock at night is midnight and twelve o'clock in the day is noon. The time between midnight and noon is a.m., short for anti meridiem, and the time between noon and midnight is p.m., short for post meridiem. So seven in the morning is written 7 a.m. and seven in the evening 7 p.m. An example rewrites the sun rising at six o'clock as 6 a.m. and a dinner at eight o'clock as 8 p.m. The next page shows why there are twenty-four hours: the hour hand takes twelve hours to go round once and goes round twice in a day. Exercise 10.2 begins with two questions this topic serves: write four times with a.m. or p.m., and tick a.m. or p.m. for four things we do in a day.
important_points: A day has 24 hours, and the hour hand goes round the clock twice.
12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight.
The time from midnight to noon is a.m.
The time from noon to midnight is p.m.
Noon and midnight are never written with a.m. or p.m.

Real objects keep their natural colours, and the ground is #FFFDF7. A date is written in boxes, a day box, a month box and a year box. A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, with the first day of the month in the right column. Countable things are at most thirty to a frame, drawn large enough to count at a glance, separated and never overlapping one another. Empty space is better than a crowded picture. Scenes in order, each with the exact narration to speak: Scene 1. Picture: A cream ground. A flat drawn notice board in its natural colours holds a card that reads Fair open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Under the board a day strip runs left to right with a sky blue left half and an amber right half and noon notched in the middle. A bus stands at the end of the strip with a question mark over its window. Narration: A fair opens at nine in the morning. It closes at five in the evening. How long is the fair open? And if a bus ride takes some hours, when does it end? Let us find out. Scene 2. Picture: A green bar is laid along the day strip from the 9 a.m. mark to the 5 p.m. mark. It is cut at noon into two pieces: the left piece is labelled From 9 a.m. to noon is 3 hours, and the right piece is labelled From noon to 5 p.m. is 5 hours. Under the strip: 3 + 5 = 8 hours in green, and the line From 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. is 8 hours. Narration: Count up to noon first. From nine in the morning to noon is three hours. Then count on from noon. From noon to five in the evening is five hours. Three hours and five hours make eight hours. The fair is open for eight hours. Scene 3. Picture: The green bar slides back to the start. A small wall clock at the 9 a.m. mark reads 9:00 with a sky blue a.m. tag. The bar steps forward eight times, one hour tile at a time, and a small wall clock at the end of the bar reads 5:00 with an amber p.m. tag. Under the strip: 9 a.m. plus 8 hours is 5 p.m. in green. Narration: We can check the answer by adding. Start at nine in the morning. Add eight hours, one hour at a time. We land on five in the evening. The check works. Scene 4. Picture: A bus on the day strip leaves a stop sign marked 1:20 p.m. A vermilion bar of 3 hours moves the bus to a second sign reading 4:20 p.m., with the line 1:20 p.m. plus 3 hours is 4:20 p.m. A short deep blue bar of 30 minutes moves it on to a third sign reading 4:50 p.m., with the line 4:20 p.m. plus 30 minutes is 4:50 p.m. Under the strip in green: 1:20 p.m. plus 3 hours 30 minutes is 4:50 p.m. Narration: A bus leaves at one twenty in the afternoon. The ride takes three hours thirty minutes. When does it arrive? Add the hours first. One twenty and three hours is four twenty. Then add the thirty minutes. The bus arrives at four fifty. Scene 5. Picture: On the day strip a film reel marker starts at the 11:10 a.m. mark in the sky blue half. A vermilion bar of 2 hours carries it across the noon notch to 1:10 p.m. in the amber half, and the tag on the sign changes from a.m. to p.m. as it crosses. A short deep blue bar of 20 minutes carries it to 1:30 p.m. Under the strip: 11:10 a.m. plus 2 hours is 1:10 p.m., then 1:10 p.m. plus 20 minutes is 1:30 p.m., in green. Narration: A film starts at ten past eleven in the morning. It lasts two hours twenty minutes. Add two hours. The clock passes noon. The morning changes to the afternoon. Then add twenty minutes. The film ends at half past one in the afternoon. Scene 6. Picture: The day strip appears with the green bar for how long and the two bars for the end time, sky blue and amber halves shown, and a small bus and film reel at the two end marks. The words Time Converter appear at the end. Narration: Let us remember. To find how long, count up to noon and then on. To find the end, add the hours and then the minutes. Next, open Time Converter. Work out how long and when it ends. The last line of the video names the tool, the Time Converter, and the video ends there.
media.instructions_for_student: Watch and listen to the whole video. Then say how you would find how long something took and how you would find when it ends.

media.title: Time Converter
media.context: Grade 3, the second half of the time chapter. An adult sees sums with 60 and 24 in them. What is actually being settled is what those two numbers are: sixty small steps in an hour and twenty-four hours in a day, and that a length of time is a stretch laid along a clock, which has to be counted in two pieces when it crosses noon. A child who learned the rule alone will multiply by 60 for days, or subtract 10 from 3 for a match that runs from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

writeup.why: Change hours into minutes and days into hours with an hour filling and a day turning, find how long something takes by laying a bar along a day strip through noon, and find when something ends by sliding the bar.
writeup.look: A wall clock and a stopwatch at the left with a row of twelve five-minute tiles under them, a day strip of twenty-four hour tiles along the foot with a green bar laid on it, a column board, and on the third phase a row of six small clocks.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Time Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the minutes, hours or days now on the stage. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The real wall clock is 280 across at x 90, y 230, with its twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and its vermilion hour hand and deep blue minute hand, drawn exactly. The real stopwatch is a round brass face 130 across at x 400, y 240 with a start button on top. The row of twelve five-minute tiles runs at x 400, y 400, each tile 44 by 60 with a 6 gap, empty until the minute hand is dragged round, and labelled 5, 10 and on to 60 as it fills, with the words one hour at its end. The train ticket card or the calendar page card stands at x 690, y 232, 320 by 150, drawn as a real ticket or a real calendar page with its words and numbers. The day strip runs along the foot at x 90, y 610, twenty-four tiles each 40 by 50 with no gap, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m. and the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., with a notch and the words 12 noon between them and the words 12 midnight at both ends. The green bar is 40 tall at y 548, laid by dragging its two ends, and it is drawn in two pieces with their two lengths written above when it crosses noon. The column board stands at x 780, y 400, 240 by 150, an hours column and a minutes column with a carry slot above each. On the third phase six small clocks, each 100 across, stand in a row at x 90, y 240 in place of the wall clock, each with a tag that reads minutes after the start. On the fourth phase the flight card or the school bell card stands in the place of the ticket. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys, a colon key and two keys labelled a.m. and p.m., for typing a count of minutes, hours or days or a time with a.m. or p.m. into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.

writeup.delight: Two small surprises. On the first phase, as the minute hand sweeps round, each five-minute tile fills with a small tick of the stopwatch and the last tile closes the row with the stopwatch button popping up. On the third and fourth phases, the green bar crosses noon and splits into two pieces that slide together into one total, and slid backwards they split again.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the wall clock stands with both hands at twelve, the row of twelve five-minute tiles is empty, and a train ticket card names a journey of some hours and minutes. On the second the day wheel stands with its sky blue half and its amber half and a calendar page card names a holiday of some days. On the third the day strip carries a start and an end across noon, a green bar waits beside it, and a row of six small clocks stands ready. On the fourth the green bar of the time taken waits at the start of the strip and a flight or a school bell card names the start. One thing moves, once: the minute hand, the wheel or the bar gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any count of hours, minutes or days on the clock and the wheel, the green bar slid along the day strip, and the column board. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on choosing minutes or hours, days into hours, a class that ends at noon, a lunch break, bottles filled in a minute, a night's sleep in a day, a school race on a stopwatch and when a school bell rings, each on a real thing.
voiceLines: A clock, a stopwatch and a day strip. Let us count the time.
One round of the minute hand fills an hour. How many minutes are in it?
The wheel turns once for one day. How many hours is that? Now for each day.
Lay the bar from the start to the end. Count to noon, then on from noon.
Slide the bar from the start. Add the hours first. Then the minutes. Which side of noon is it?
A new time to work out. What is it about?
Free play. Fill an hour, turn a day and slide the bar as you like.
Count again, one step at a time. Which side of noon are you on?
You counted the time with the hour filling and the day turning.

observations.why: the minute hand moves five minutes from one number to the next, and twelve fives make sixty.
observations.soWhat: an hour is sixty minutes, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by sixty.
observations.observe: One round of the minute hand filled twelve five-minute tiles and the row read sixty.

observations.why: the hour hand goes round twice in a day, once for the a.m. half and once for the p.m. half.
observations.soWhat: a day is twenty-four hours, so days change into hours by multiplying by twenty-four.
observations.observe: The day wheel turned once and counted twenty-four hour tiles, twelve sky blue and twelve amber.

observations.why: the day strip has a notch at noon, and the part before it and the part after it are counted apart.
observations.soWhat: to find how long something takes across noon, count to noon and from noon, and add.
observations.observe: A bar that crossed noon split into two pieces and the two lengths added up to the whole.

observations.why: the bar is as long as the time taken, so its end is the start plus that time.
observations.soWhat: to find when something ends, add the time taken to the start time, hours first and then minutes.
observations.observe: Sliding the bar from the start put its end on the time the thing finishes.

source_tool.description: A real wall clock, 280 across, stands at the left of the working area, with its twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and an hour hand and a minute hand, the hour hand vermilion and the minute hand deep blue. Beside it stands a real stopwatch with a round face and a start button. A row of twelve five-minute tiles runs under them, each tile 44 across. When the minute hand is dragged once round the clock the tiles fill one at a time, labelled 5, 10 and on to 60, until the row reads sixty minutes and a small label says one hour. Along the foot of the working area runs a day strip of twenty-four hour tiles, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m., the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., with a notch and the words 12 noon between them. A green bar the child sets by dragging its two ends is laid along the strip to show a length of time, and it is drawn in two pieces, with the two lengths written above them, when it crosses noon. Sliding the whole bar along the strip moves its end. A column board with an hours column and a minutes column takes a sum, with a carry shown above the column it joins. On the third phase a row of six small clocks, each reading a finishing time as minutes after a start, replaces the wall clock, and the child taps the longest and the shortest. A number pad sets any count and types any answer. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many minutes, hours or days are on the stage.
