style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count again, one step at a time. Which side of noon are you on?
voice.onNext: A new time to work out. What is it about?
voice.opening: A clock, a stopwatch and a day strip. Let us count the time.
voice.onFinish: You counted the time with the hour filling and the day turning.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Fill an hour, turn a day and slide the bar as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Sixty minutes make an hour
Twenty-four hours make a day
How long did it take?
When will it end?

placement.where: After the class has timed one minute with a stopwatch, writing or clapping, and has sat a paper plate clock at the start and the end of a lesson. The tool is what fills an hour with sixty marks and lays a length of time along a whole day, which a paper plate cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by 60, and an hour and some minutes is changed by changing the hours and adding the minutes. There are 24 hours in a day, so days change into hours by multiplying by 24. To find how long something takes, count from the start to noon and from noon to the end, and add the two parts; if it does not cross noon, count straight across. To find when something ends, add the time taken to the start time, hours first and then minutes, and write a.m. or p.m. by which side of noon the end falls on. Noon and midnight take neither a.m. nor p.m.
answer_key.wrong: The hour fills again slowly, one five-minute tile at a time, or the bar is laid along the day strip again and cut at noon into its two pieces, and the pieces are counted aloud. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: One hour is 60 minutes.
Change the hours first: 9 hours is 540 minutes.
Then add the 10 minutes. 540 plus 10 is 550.
So 9 hours 10 minutes is 550 minutes.
items.question: A train ticket shows a journey of 9 hours 10 minutes. How many minutes is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the hours into minutes first, then add the minutes.
items.misconception: Writing 910 by joining the 9 and the 10, or forgetting to change the hours at all.

steps: One day is 24 hours.
8 days is 8 times 24 hours.
8 times 24 is 192.
So 8 days is 192 hours.
items.question: A calendar page shows a holiday that lasts 8 days. How many hours is that?
items.checkpoint: A day has 24 hours, so multiply the days by 24.
items.misconception: Multiplying by 60, the minutes in an hour, because the last answer was done with 60.

steps: Count from 10 a.m. to 12 noon: 2 hours.
Then count from 12 noon to 3 p.m.: 3 hours.
Add the two parts: 2 plus 3 is 5.
So from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. is 5 hours.
items.question: A cricket match starts at 10 a.m. and ends at 3 p.m. How long does the match last?
items.checkpoint: Count to noon first, then on from noon, and add the two parts.
items.misconception: Taking 10 from 3, or counting 3 minus 10 as if the clock never passed noon.

steps: Add the hours first: 9:20 a.m. plus 3 hours is 12:20 p.m.
Then add the 45 minutes: 12:20 p.m. plus 45 minutes is 1:05 p.m.
The time passed noon, so it is p.m.
So the flight lands at 1:05 p.m.
items.question: A flight leaves at 9:20 a.m. and takes 3 hours 45 minutes. When does the flight land?
items.checkpoint: Add the hours first, then the minutes, and say a.m. or p.m. by which side of noon it is.
items.misconception: Writing 12:65 for the minutes, or keeping a.m. after the time has passed noon.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A child brushes teeth with a toothbrush and then sleeps in a bed all night. Which unit fits brushing teeth, minutes or hours? Which unit fits a night's sleep?
items.final_answer: Minutes fit brushing teeth, and hours fit a night's sleep

items.question: A bus tour on a calendar page lasts 10 days. How many hours is that?
items.final_answer: 240 hours, because 1 day is 24 hours and 10 times 24 is 240

items.question: A story class starts at 11 a.m. and ends at 12 noon. How long is the class?
items.final_answer: 1 hour, because from 11 a.m. to 12 noon is 1 hour

items.question: The school bell rings for lunch at 12 noon. Lunch lasts 1 hour. When does lunch end?
items.final_answer: 1 p.m., because 12 noon plus 1 hour is 1 p.m.

items.question: A child fills 3 bottles with a mug in 1 minute, timed on a stopwatch. How many bottles can the child fill in 1 hour at the same speed?
items.final_answer: 180 bottles, because 1 hour is 60 minutes and 3 times 60 is 180

items.question: A child sleeps in a bed for 9 hours each night. A day has 24 hours. How many hours of the day is the child awake?
items.final_answer: 15 hours, because 24 take away 9 is 15

items.question: Two children start a pot painting race at 12 noon and a stopwatch times them. The first stops at 12:25 p.m. and the second stops at 1:05 p.m. How much longer did the second child take?
items.final_answer: 40 minutes longer. From 12 noon to 12:25 p.m. is 25 minutes, and from 12 noon to 1:05 p.m. is 65 minutes

items.question: A child leaves home at 7:20 a.m. and takes 25 minutes to walk to school. The child reaches the gate 10 minutes before the school bell rings. When does the bell ring?
items.final_answer: 7:55 a.m., because 7:20 a.m. plus 25 minutes is 7:45 a.m., and the bell rings 10 minutes later

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: drags once round the wall clock, and the five-minute tiles fill one at a time
turns once through the twenty-four hour tiles, the a.m. half sky blue and the p.m. half amber
drag to lay a green bar along the day strip from a start to an end
moves the whole bar along the strip so its end shows when something ends
takes a sum of hours and minutes with the carry shown above the column
shows six small clocks as minutes after a start, and the child taps the longest and the shortest
types any count of hours, minutes or days and any answer

media.teaching_notes: Time one minute with a stopwatch before the tool opens: write the school name, clap, or fill bottles with a mug and a funnel, and count. Say that an hour is sixty of those minutes, and let a paper plate clock turn once to show it. Lay a long paper strip marked in twenty-four hours with noon in the middle, colour the morning half sky blue and the evening half amber, and lay a strip of card along it from a start to an end. When the card crosses noon, cut it there and add the two pieces, and wait for the child to say why before you show the rule. Write noon as 12 noon and midnight as 12 midnight, and never give either of them a.m. or p.m. Use fresh times: the exercise's shifts, films and practice sessions are the child's own to work.
media.generation_prompt: Build a time conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A real wall clock, 280 across, stands at the left of the working area with twelve numbers, sixty minute marks, a vermilion hour hand and a deep blue minute hand, and a real stopwatch stands beside it. A row of twelve five-minute tiles runs under them and fills one tile at a time as the minute hand is dragged once round, until it reads sixty minutes. A day strip of twenty-four hour tiles runs along the foot, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m., the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., noon notched between them. A green bar with two draggable ends is laid along the strip to show a length of time, and is drawn in two pieces with their two lengths written above them when it crosses noon, and the whole bar slides along the strip to show an end time. A column board with an hours column and a minutes column takes sums with the carry shown above the column it joins. On the third phase a row of six small clocks reading minutes after a start replaces the wall clock and the child taps the longest and the shortest. A number pad types counts and answers. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the minutes, hours or days on the stage. Noon and midnight never carry a.m. or p.m. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
media.instructions_for_student: Fill the hour with sixty minutes. Turn the day wheel. Lay the green bar along the day. Slide it to find when it ends.

media.title: Twenty-Four Hours Make a Day
media.context: Shown on the second concept of the fourth topic, where days are changed into hours by counting twenty-fours.
media.description: A brown suitcase stands to the left of a row of six equal rounded square cream tiles. Each tile contains a yellow sun with eight rays above a pale circular moon. Beneath the first tile, a dark blue bracket spans its width, labelled with the text "1 day: 24 hours". Under all six tiles, a long green bracket stretches from the left of the first tile to the right of the sixth tile, labelled with the text "6 days". Centred underneath that bracket is the text "6 days is 144 hours".

source_image.note: Authored for this plan; no source asset supplied.

media.teaching_notes: Ask how many hours are in one day and how many days the holiday lasts. Say that 6 days is six twenty-fours, 144 hours. If a child adds 6 and 24, ask how many hours there are in each of the six days.

Create a high-quality educational visual for NCERT/Udgam Mathematics, for students aged 8 to 9. It must be clean, sharp, easy to understand and spacious, and it explains one idea only.

Teaching purpose: A holiday lasts 6 days. One day is 24 hours, so 6 days is six twenty-fours, which is 144 hours.

Look:
- Plain warm white background with generous white space on every side. No panels, boxes, borders, shadows or decoration other than the title banner.
- A simple title banner runs across the top: a pale blue rounded strip about one seventh of the frame height, with the title text "Twenty-Four Hours Make a Day" in large bold deep-blue type on one line. The strip starts at the left margin and stops about one seventh of the frame width short of the right edge, so the top-right corner stays empty, because a logo is added there later. No sparkles, underline strokes, icons or other decoration on or around the banner.
- Clean flat vector style: crisp even fills, one consistent near-black outline weight, no gradients, no texture, no 3D, and no perspective unless the composition below asks for it.
- Colour carries meaning: the long bracket is green, because it holds the answer, 144 hours. Real objects keep their natural colours; the colour roles are carried by the hands, tags and bands.
- The suitcase and the day tiles are flat vector drawings. Each tile shows the same sun and moon, to say that a day holds a day and a night.
- Text is only the four labels below, in a clean bold rounded sans-serif that reads easily at half size, with correct spelling and spacing.

Composition (centred, with wide margins):
- The title banner sits at the top. Everything else sits in the space below it.
- The suitcase is small at the left and the six tiles run in one straight row of equal tiles with equal gaps.

Labels to render, spelled exactly as written:
- Twenty-Four Hours Make a Day (the title, in the banner, written once)
- 1 day: 24 hours
- 6 days
- 6 days is 144 hours

Accuracy constraints:
- Exactly six tiles, each with one sun and one moon, and exactly one suitcase.
- 6 times 24 is 144. No clock face, digital time or date is drawn.

The frame is wrong if it shows:
- Given, Step, Result, Wrong or Right panels, boxes or banners other than the title banner

media.title: How Long Did It Take?
media.context: Shown on the third concept of the fourth topic, where a length of time is counted through noon and added.
media.description: Beside a small brick school and a hanging bell sit two round clocks. The left clock shows 8:00 with a blue minute hand on 12 and a vermilion hour hand on 8, labelled "8 a.m." beneath. The right clock shows 2:00 with a blue minute hand on 12 and a vermilion hour hand on 2, labelled "2 p.m." beneath. Below them, a horizontal bar is split into a light blue section labelled "4 hours" and an amber section labelled "2 hours", separated by a mark labelled "noon". A green bracket runs under the bar, labelled "4 plus 2 is 6 hours".

source_image.note: Authored for this plan; no source asset supplied.

media.teaching_notes: Ask how long it is from 8 a.m. to noon, then from noon to 2 p.m., and how long the school day is altogether. Say we count to noon first, then add. If a child subtracts 2 from 8, ask them to follow the band through noon.

topics.detailed_summary: Two sentences about a metro journey mean the same: it takes about sixty minutes, and it takes about one hour. The minute hand takes one hour, or sixty minutes, to go round the clock once, so there are sixty minutes in an hour, and the hour hand goes round twice, so there are twenty-four hours in a day. Examples change days into hours by multiplying by twenty-four, hours into minutes by multiplying by sixty, and an hour and a half into ninety minutes. A security guard works from eight in the morning to four in the afternoon, and the length of the shift is found by counting from eight to noon and from noon to four, four hours and four hours, eight hours in all. A film starts at half past three and lasts two hours, so it ends at half past five, and football practice from half past four to half past six lasts two hours. Exercise 10.2 continues with seven questions: choose minutes or hours for six activities, calculate six conversions, tick the sensible length of time for five things, change three and a half hours into minutes, work out how long a nursery class lasts, and two Critical Thinking problems about a train journey in hours and about when a school bell rings. The last page asks four questions about the finishing times of six bears, and the Math Lab Activity finds how long one minute is by writing, clapping and filling bottles for a minute.
important_points: 1 hour is 60 minutes, and 1 day is 24 hours.
To change hours into minutes, multiply by 60. To change days into hours, multiply by 24.
To find how long something takes, count from the start time to the end time, through noon if needed.
To find the end time, add the time taken to the start time.
A minute is a short time. It is about how many times you can clap or write a name in one minute.

media.title: Writing Dates
media.context: Plays first in this topic, on its own watch concept, before the tool. It explains the whole topic in four short parts, one for each concept, and ends by sending the child to the tool.
media.description: A narrated, animated explainer of about 92 seconds, in the chapter's flat picture-book style, spoken in plain words with short sentences. A school diary page carries the date nine March, twenty twenty-seven, with a day, a month and a year. Written the Day-Month-Year way, the day comes first, then the month in words, then the year. Written the DD-MM-YYYY way, the day and the month take two digits each, so the date is 09-03-2027, with March as the third month. A second date, 18-06-2014, is read back into words as eighteen June, twenty fourteen, because the sixth month is June. It ends by sending the child to the Write the Date tool.
media.teaching_notes: Play it once before the tool is opened. Afterwards ask three things: which three parts a date has, which way writes the month in words, and how many digits the day, the month and the year take in the way that uses only numbers. Have a month ladder from 01 to 12 to hand. The tool brings its own new dates, so nothing in the video is a question from it.

One calm, friendly English voice speaks at a slow, even pace, and leaves a two second silence after every question before the answer. The words are written for the ear: short sentences, plain words, every number said in words. Show on screen what the voice is saying, as it says it. On-screen text is only labels, numerals and symbols, and never a copy of the narration. No brand names, no faces, no cartoon characters, no music. Picture rules for this chapter: Flat, friendly primary-school picture-book illustration of REAL everyday things that tell or mark time, each one recognisable at a glance and drawn in its own natural colours: a wall clock, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a brass school bell, a stopwatch, a wall calendar page, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a birthday card. Clean vector shapes, even fills, a single consistent line weight, no gradients, no drop shadows, no texture. Every clock is exact: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand six degrees a minute, the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute. Neither hand has an arrowhead and the two hands never lie on top of each other where the child is to read them. The clock face, rim and numbers are near-black #2B2B2B on cream. A time is written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone. Noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m. A length of time is a bar laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end. A bar that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces, and the two pieces are added. Colour code, used consistently in every frame of this chapter. The hour hand and the hours are vermilion #D55E00. The minute hand and the minutes are deep blue #0072B2. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue #56B4E9. The p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber #E69F00. The time reached, a length of time worked out and the answer are green #009E73. Real objects keep their natural colours, and the ground is #FFFDF7. A date is written in boxes, a day box, a month box and a year box. A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, with the first day of the month in the right column. Countable things are at most thirty to a frame, drawn large enough to count at a glance, separated and never overlapping one another. Empty space is better than a crowded picture. Scenes in order, each with the exact narration to speak: Scene 1. Picture: A cream ground. A flat drawn school diary lies open in its natural colours with the date 9 March 2027 written across the top of the page in near-black. A question mark floats over the date. Narration: Look at the date on this diary page. How many things does a date tell us? Let us find out. Scene 2. Picture: The date lifts off the page into three rounded boxes in a row, each outlined in near-black and labelled under it: 9 in the box labelled Day, March in the box labelled Month, 2027 in the box labelled Year. Narration: A date has three parts. Nine is the day. March is the month. Twenty twenty-seven is the year. A date always has all three. Scene 3. Picture: Numbered arrows 1, 2, 3 run over the three boxes from left to right. Under them the date 9 March 2027 is written in full and takes the label Day-Month-Year. The month box has a small tag in words. Narration: This is the Day-Month-Year way. Write the day first. Then write the month in words. Then write the year. Nine March, twenty twenty-seven. Scene 4. Picture: A month ladder runs down the side from 01 January to 12 December, and the row 03 March lights. The three boxes change to two boxes of two digits and one box of four digits: 09, 03 and 2027, with hyphens between them, so the date reads 09-03-2027. A near-black bracket under each box is labelled DD, MM and YYYY. A small zero in the first box slides in front of the 9. Narration: There is another way to write a date, using only numbers. The day takes two digits, so nine becomes zero nine. March is the third month, so the month is zero three. The year takes four digits. Zero nine, zero three, twenty twenty-seven. Hyphens go between the parts. Scene 5. Picture: A second diary page carries 18-06-2014 in three boxes. The month box 06 slides down the ladder to the row 06 June and turns into the word June, so the page reads 18 June 2014. A toggle switches the date between 18-06-2014 and 18 June 2014, and a green equals sign appears between the two forms. Narration: Read this date. The day is eighteen. The month is zero six. Zero six is the sixth month. It is June. The year is twenty fourteen. It is eighteen June, twenty fourteen. Both ways tell the same date. Scene 6. Picture: The two diary pages stand side by side, one showing the date in words and one in numbers, with the month ladder between them. The words Write the Date appear at the end. Narration: Let us remember. A date has a day, a month and a year. We can write the month in words or as two digits. Next, open Write the Date. Build a date in boxes. The last line of the video names the tool, the Write the Date, and the video ends there.

voiceLines: A card with a date on it, and three empty boxes. Let us write it down.
A date has three parts. Which is the day? Which is the month? Which is the year?
Write the day first. Then spell the month out. Then the year. Read it aloud.
Find the month on the ladder. Its number goes in the middle. Two digits, two digits, four digits.
Say the date the other way. Turn the toggle. Do both ways name one day?
A new card. What is its day, its month and its year?
Free play. Write any date, and turn it between words and numbers.
Look at the labels under the boxes. Which part goes where?
You wrote the date in words and in numbers, and both said the same day.

observations.why: a date is made of three parts, and every part has its own place.
observations.soWhat: a date has a day, a month and a year, and all three are needed.
observations.observe: The day, the month and the year each had a box with a label under it.

observations.why: the ladder lists the twelve months, and the Day-Month-Year way writes the month in words.
observations.soWhat: Day-Month-Year writes the day, then the month in words, then the year.
observations.observe: The month name dropped into the middle box when it was tapped on the ladder.

observations.why: the number is the month's place in the year, and DD-MM-YYYY writes it with two digits.
observations.soWhat: DD-MM-YYYY writes two digits for the day, two for the month and four for the year.
observations.observe: The ladder showed a number beside every month, and the month box took two digits.

observations.why: the two ways write the same three parts, only the month is written differently.
observations.soWhat: a date in words and the same date in numbers name one date, so both are correct.
observations.observe: The toggle turned the date from words to numbers and the same day stayed on the card.

media.description: Fill the day, month and year boxes on a real card, spell the month in words or write it in numbers, and turn a date from one way into the other.

mods.learn: Learn, adult alongside. Four worked items, one per phase, from the three parts of a date on a birthday card to a diary date turned back into words.
mods.freeplay: Free Play. Any date the calendar allows in the three boxes, the toggle between the month in words and the month in numbers, and the month ladder.
mods.practice: Practice, child alone. Eight items on the parts of a date, the month in words, the month in numbers with two digits, a date that cannot be real, and dates turned from numbers into words and back, each on a real card or ticket.

source_tool.name: Write the Date
source_tool.blurb: Fill the day, month and year boxes on a real card, spell the month in words or write it in numbers, and turn a date from one way into the other.

writing three dates with the names of the months

source_tool.description: A real card stands at the left of the working area, 560 by 300: a birthday card, an invitation or a school notice, drawn as a recognisable flat illustration in its natural colours with a line of words on it that names the event. Under its words sit three rounded boxes in a row, a day box 120 wide, a month box 220 wide and a year box 160 wide, each with its label beneath it, Day, Month and Year. A month ladder stands at the right, twelve small tiles in two columns of six, each tile 150 by 54 and holding a month name and its number, January 01 down to December 12. A toggle button labelled Month in words and Month in numbers turns the same date between the two ways of writing it: in the first the boxes read as in 7 November, and in the second they read as in 07-11, with the dashes drawn between the boxes. A pad types the day, the month number and the year. A short line in words under the card says when a date is not a real one, and why. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many boxes are filled.
source_tool.art_direction: A birthday card on a classroom desk / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the labels under the boxes. Which part goes where?
voice.onNext: A new card. What is its day, its month and its year?
voice.opening: A card with a date on it, and three empty boxes. Let us write it down.
voice.onFinish: You wrote the date in words and in numbers, and both said the same day.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Write any date, and turn it between words and numbers.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A date has a day, a month and a year
Day-Month-Year: the month in words
DD-MM-YYYY: the month in numbers
From words to numbers and back

placement.where: After each child has written their own birthday on a card in words, and then in numbers, and swapped it with a partner who has read it aloud. The tool is what turns one date between the two ways with a single toggle, and what refuses a date that is not real, which a card cannot do for itself.

answer_key.rule: A date has a day, a month and a year. Day-Month-Year writes the month in words, as in 7 November 2019. DD-MM-YYYY writes the month in numbers, as in 07-11-2019, with two digits for the day, two for the month and four for the year, and the month number is its place in the year, January 01 to December 12. The two ways name the same date, so both are correct. A date must be a real one: no month has more days than it has.
answer_key.wrong: The boxes are shown again with their labels, Day, Month and Year, and the month ladder lights the month the child wrote beside its number, so the part that was misplaced is seen in its own box. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A date has three parts: the day, the month and the year.
The first number, 23, is the day.
The word March is the month.
The last number, 2017, is the year.
items.answer: The day is 23, the month is March and the year is 2017
items.question: A birthday card says 23 March 2017. Which number is the day, which word is the month and which number is the year?
items.checkpoint: A date always has a day, a month and a year.
items.misconception: Calling 2017 the day because it is the biggest number.

steps: Day-Month-Year writes the day first.
Then write the month in words: August.
Then write the year: 2013.
So the date is 9 August 2013.
items.question: An invitation card has the day 9, the month August and the year 2013. Write the date with the month in words.
items.checkpoint: Write the day, then the month in words, then the year.
items.misconception: Writing 2013 first, or leaving the month out and writing only 9 2013.

steps: DD is the day, so write 14.
MM is the month. On the ladder, October is the 10th month, so write 10.
YYYY is the year, so write 2019.
Put dashes between them. The date is 14-10-2019.
items.question: A school notice board shows 14 October 2019. Write the date in numbers as DD-MM-YYYY.
items.checkpoint: Two digits for the day, two for the month and four for the year, with the month's number from the ladder.
items.misconception: Writing the month as 10 but the day as 4, or putting 14-2019-10 in the wrong order.

steps: DD-MM-YYYY: the first part is the day, 05, which is 5.
The second part is the month, 12. On the ladder, 12 is December.
The last part is the year, 2021.
So 05-12-2021 is 5 December 2021.
items.question: A diary page says 05-12-2021. Write the date with the month in words.
items.checkpoint: Read the first part as the day and the second part as the month, then find the month on the ladder.
items.misconception: Reading 05-12-2021 as 12 May, because the first number looks like the month.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A train ticket shows the day 30, the month April and the year 2015. Which of the three is the year?
items.final_answer: 2015 is the year

items.question: A library card says it was made on the 17th of June 2012. Write the date as Day-Month-Year.
items.final_answer: 17 June 2012

items.question: An exam admit card is for the month of September. Which two digits go in the month box of DD-MM-YYYY?
items.final_answer: 09, because September is the 9th month

items.question: A calendar page is marked 28-02-2018. Write the date with the month in words.
items.final_answer: 28 February 2018

items.question: A sports day poster on a notice board says 31 November 2016. Can that be a real date? Why?
items.final_answer: No. November has 30 days, so there is no 31st of November

items.question: A report card shows 5 March 2016. A child writes 5-3-2016 in the DD-MM-YYYY boxes. What must change?
items.final_answer: 05-03-2016, because the day and the month each need two digits

items.question: A train ticket says 12-04-2023. A child reads it as 4 December 2023. Is that right? Say the date correctly.
items.final_answer: No. The first part is the day and the second part is the month, so 12-04-2023 is 12 April 2023

items.question: A school notice board has the dates 21-09-2013 and 9 September 2013. Do they name the same date?
items.final_answer: No. 21-09-2013 is 21 September 2013, and the other is 9 September 2013

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: take the three parts of a date from the pad
lists January to December with the numbers 01 to 12, and lights a month when tapped
turns the same date between the month in words and the month in numbers
types the day, the month number and the year
reads the boxes back against the card and says in words if a date is not real

media.teaching_notes: Before the tool opens, ask each child to write their own birthday on a card with the month in words, and on a second card in numbers, using a list of the twelve months with their numbers beside them, and to read both aloud to a partner. Wait for the child to say which part is the day, which the month and which the year before you name the two ways. The month number is its place in the year: January is the first month and December the twelfth, and the ladder is there to be looked at, not memorised. Say that both ways are correct and name the same date. A date that does not exist is not a mistake of writing but of the calendar, so ask how many days the month has. Use fresh dates: the exercise's dates and years are the child's own to write.

A month ladder of twelve tiles in two columns of six, each 150 by 54, lists January 01 down to December 12 at the right. A toggle button turns the date between the month in words, as in 7 November 2019, and the month in numbers, as in 07-11-2019 with dashes between the boxes. MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Create a high-quality educational visual for NCERT/Udgam Mathematics, for students aged 8 to 9. It must be clean, sharp, easy to understand and spacious, and it explains one idea only.

Teaching purpose: The Day-Month-Year way writes the day first, then the month in words, then the year: 7 November 2019.

Look:
- Plain warm white background with generous white space on every side. No panels, boxes, borders, shadows or decoration other than the title banner.
- A simple title banner runs across the top: a pale blue rounded strip about one seventh of the frame height, with the title text "Day-Month-Year" in large bold deep-blue type on one line. The strip starts at the left margin and stops about one seventh of the frame width short of the right edge, so the top-right corner stays empty, because a logo is added there later. No sparkles, underline strokes, icons or other decoration on or around the banner.
- Clean flat vector style: crisp even fills, one consistent near-black outline weight, no gradients, no texture, no 3D, and no perspective unless the composition below asks for it.
- Colour carries meaning: none here. The three tags are the same white. Real objects keep their natural colours; the colour roles are carried by the hands, tags and bands.
- The notebook is a flat vector drawing of a real notebook page. The date is printed type, not handwriting.
- Text is only the five labels below, in a clean bold rounded sans-serif that reads easily at half size, with correct spelling and spacing.

Composition (centred, with wide margins):
- The title banner sits at the top. Everything else sits in the space below it.
- The date line is large and centred near the top of the page, with the three tags in one row below it.
- Each tag sits directly under the part it names, and nothing overlaps.

Labels to render, spelled exactly as written:
- Day-Month-Year (the title, in the banner, written once)
- 7 November 2019
- Day first
- Month in words
- Year last

Accuracy constraints:
- The line reads exactly 7 November 2019, with the month spelled November.
- Exactly three tags, in the order Day first, Month in words, Year last.

The frame is wrong if it shows:
- Given, Step, Result, Wrong or Right panels, boxes or banners other than the title banner
- the date written as numbers only, such as 07-11-2019
- a different date, or a weekday name
- a person, a hand or a pen
- a second or altered title, a logo or a watermark
- any person, hand or face

media.context: Grade 3, the last working topic of the time chapter. An adult sees a calendar being flipped, which a paper calendar can do. What is being settled is that a week is always seven days so the same weekday returns every seventh day, that months take turns on the knuckles and in the dips, and that a leap year comes every fourth year and not at random. A child who counts the days between two dates by counting both ends, or who counts forward without taking away the first day, will be one day out and will not see why.

writeup.why: Count the days of a week and the months of a year on a real wall calendar, say the days of each month by the knuckle method, find the leap year as every fourth year, and hop seven days at a time to find a day, a date and the weeks between two dates.
writeup.look: A classroom wall with a real calendar page of 2026 at the left, the month cards, the two fists, the four-year strip and the week counter at the right as each phase needs them, a pencil, flip arrows, a Grid view button, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Calendar Explorer' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many days, weeks or months have been counted so far. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A real wall calendar page hangs at the left of the working area at x 90, y 216, 470 by 440, with a near-black top bar showing the month and the year written large, a header row of the seven days of the week with Sunday first, and a grid of dates in seven columns, the first of the month standing in its true column and a week sharing a row. Two round arrow buttons stand under it at x 90 and x 220, y 668, each 120 by 52, and flip the page like a leaf, and a pencil rests at its right edge. The Grid view button stands at x 360, y 668, 200 by 52, and redraws the page as a plain table. Beside the page, at x 600, y 216, a work area 520 by 440 changes with the phase. On the first phase a row of twelve small month cards, two rows of six each 80 by 70, stands at x 600, y 216, and the week counter, 240 by 100, stands at x 600, y 330. On the second phase two flat drawn fists stand side by side at x 600, y 230, each 240 by 220: the first with four knuckles and three dips labelled January, March, May, July and February, April, June, the second with three knuckles and two dips labelled August, October, December and September, November, and the twelve month cards wait in a row at x 600, y 480, 520 by 90; a card dropped on a knuckle reads thirty-one and on a dip reads thirty, and February is left with its two numbers. On the third phase a four-year strip of four small wall calendars stands at x 600, y 230, 520 by 190, showing their Februaries side by side, the leap year's with a twenty-ninth square ringed in green and labelled Leap year, and the year ruler from 1900 to 2099 in blocks of four runs under it at x 600, y 470, 520 by 90, with a marker the child steps in fours. On the fourth phase the circled date is ringed near-black and the date reached is ringed green, labelled Answer, the seven-day hop lights every seventh date down the same column in one colour, and the week counter stands at x 600, y 470, 260 by 120, counting the weeks between two circled dates in sevens. Real things keep their natural colours throughout, and a date found is never coloured as an hour or a minute. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing a number of days, weeks or months or a year into the answer slot, with a words box that takes the name of a day. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The calendar page shows the last date circled with the hops lit down its column, and the week counter beside it, with the fists or the strip still in the frame.

phases.win: the twelve pages stack into a year and one extra day sits after the last full week
phases.does: taps a row to count its days, flips through the twelve pages, then counts the weeks in a year and the one day left over
phases.goal: a week has seven days, a year has twelve months and is about fifty-two weeks and one more day
phases.says: Flip the pages of the calendar. How many months make a year?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a school trip lasts some weeks. How would you find how many days that is, and why is a year not exactly fifty-two weeks?
phases.feels: the pages of the year flipping past, and one day left over after the last full week
phases.hands: Hang a real wall calendar, count the days in one row with a finger, flip the pages and count the months, and ask how many weeks fit in the year.
phases.tries: First rung: count the days in one row of the calendar. Second rung: count the rows of seven that make a year. Third rung: the same task with just one month, before the whole year returns.

wrong.why: fifty-two sevens seems to fill the year with no day over
wrong.move: says a year is exactly fifty-two weeks
wrong.screen: the week counter fills with fifty-two full rows of seven, and one lone day is left lit amber on the last page, labelled Left, with the count of days written beside it

wrong.why: twelve months of the same length is easy to multiply
wrong.move: counts the days of the year by adding the twelve months and forgetting that they are not equal
wrong.screen: each month card shows its own number of days when it is tapped, and the counts are added in turn as the pages are flipped

phases.screen: the 2026 wall calendar open at its first month with a row of twelve month cards beside it and the week counter blank
phases.soWhat: a week has seven days, a year has twelve months and is fifty-two weeks and one more day
phases.concept: Days, weeks, months and a year

phases.win: the card lands and its number of days appears, and February is left alone with its two numbers
phases.does: says each month along the fists, drops the card on a knuckle or a dip, and reads the number of days
phases.goal: months take turns on the knuckles and in the dips: a knuckle month has thirty-one days and a dip month thirty
phases.says: Say the months along the knuckles and the dips. Which months have thirty-one days?
phases.check: Away from the screen: make a fist and say the months. Is the month your birthday is in on a knuckle or in a dip, and how many days does it have?
phases.feels: the months falling onto knuckles and dips in turn, with February left alone
phases.hands: Make a fist and say the months along the knuckles and the dips, then fold a paper strip into twelve boxes, mark the knuckle months and write the days in each.
phases.tries: First rung: say the months along the fist from January. Second rung: say whether the month you stopped on is a knuckle or a dip. Third rung: the same task with the first four months only, before the rest return.

wrong.why: the first months said, January and March, have thirty-one, so it feels like all of them
wrong.move: says a dip month has thirty-one days
wrong.screen: the month card is dropped on the dip and its number reads thirty, and the knuckle months light in turn along the fist with thirty-one beside each

wrong.why: two fists look like two sets of months
wrong.move: counts the knuckles and dips as if the months sat in two separate rows
wrong.screen: the months are said along the first fist and then, without a gap, along the second, so July and August both sit on a knuckle and the count carries on

phases.screen: two drawn fists with four knuckles and three dips on the first and three knuckles and two dips on the second, and twelve month cards waiting
phases.soWhat: a knuckle month has thirty-one days, a dip month has thirty, and February has twenty-eight or twenty-nine
phases.concept: How many days in a month: the knuckle method

phases.win: the twenty-ninth square drops into the leap February and the year ruler lights every fourth year
phases.does: counts in fours on the year ruler from a leap year, taps the February that grows a twenty-ninth square, and finds a year from the last and the next leap years
phases.goal: every fourth year is a leap year, and its February has an extra day and the year has one day more
phases.says: Look at the four Februaries. Which one has an extra day?
phases.check: Away from the screen: this year is a leap year. In how many years is the next one, and how many days does February have in it?
phases.feels: the extra day dropping into one February in four
phases.hands: Fold a paper strip into four boxes, one for each year, draw February in each, give one an extra day, and count in fours from a leap year on a number line of years.
phases.tries: First rung: step the marker four years from a leap year. Second rung: check that the year you land on is a leap year. Third rung: the same task with the last leap year only, before the next one returns.

wrong.why: the leap years seen so far all happened to have even numbers
wrong.move: says every year that ends in an even number is a leap year
wrong.screen: the year ruler lights every fourth year only, and the years between it stay dark even when their numbers are even

wrong.why: three or five seems close enough to a few years
wrong.move: counts in threes or fives instead of fours from a leap year
wrong.screen: the marker steps four years at a time along the ruler, and the February on the strip grows its extra square only at every fourth step

phases.screen: a four-year strip of small wall calendars with their Februaries side by side, and a year ruler from nineteen hundred to two thousand ninety-nine
phases.soWhat: every fourth year is a leap year, with twenty-nine days in February and three hundred and sixty-six days in the year
phases.concept: Leap year: every fourth year has 366 days

phases.win: the hops light the same weekday down the column and the week counter shows the weeks between the two dates
phases.does: circles a date, hops seven days at a time down the column, then counts on to the date asked for or counts the weeks between two circled dates
phases.goal: the same day of the week comes back every seven days, so a day or a date is found by hopping in sevens
phases.says: Circle the date. Hop seven days and see which day lights up each time.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a plant was put in a pot on a Monday. What day of the week is it three weeks later, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the same weekday lighting down the column, one week at a time
phases.hands: Circle a date on a real wall calendar with a pencil, count seven days along with a finger and see which day you land on, then count the days to a second date and change them into weeks.
phases.tries: First rung: hop seven days once. Second rung: hop again and say the day each time. Third rung: the same task with one hop only, before more hops return.

wrong.why: counting both ends feels natural when pointing at dates
wrong.move: counts the days between two dates including the first date
wrong.screen: the first date is ringed near-black and left out of the count, the days are counted from the next date on, and the week counter shows the total

wrong.why: a week is easy to mix up with the days that make it
wrong.move: hops six days or eight days instead of seven
wrong.screen: each hop lands on a date lit in one colour, and a hop of six or eight leaves a different weekday lit, so the seventh is seen to be the one that stays

phases.screen: a calendar page with a pencil, a seven-day hop and a week counter, and one date already circled
phases.soWhat: the same day of the week comes back every seven days, so a day or a date is found by hopping in sevens
phases.concept: Finding a day and a date on a calendar

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the pencil circles a date, the seven-day hop jumps down the calendar one week at a time, lighting the same weekday in the same colour with a small tick each time it lands. On the third phase, the leap February squeezes in its twenty-ninth square with a soft click, and the other three Februaries stay as they were.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the 2026 wall calendar is open at its first month, a row of twelve month cards lies beside it and the week counter is blank. On the second the two drawn fists stand beside the calendar with their knuckles and dips labelled and the twelve month cards waiting. On the third a four-year strip of small wall calendars shows its Februaries side by side, and the year ruler is lit at one leap year. On the fourth a calendar page has one date circled with the pencil, the seven-day hop is lit but has not yet moved, and the week counter is empty. One thing moves, once: the first page, or the circled date on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any month of the 2026 calendar, the two fists with every month card, the four-year strip and the year ruler, any circled date with the seven-day hop, and the Grid view. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the months of a year, the knuckle method, the leap year and finding a day or a date, each in a real situation.
voiceLines: A calendar on the wall, waiting to be flipped.
Flip the pages of the calendar. How many months make a year?
Say the months along the knuckles and the dips. Which months have thirty-one days?
Look at the four Februaries. Which one has an extra day?
Circle the date. Hop seven days and see which day lights up each time.
A new page. Find the day first.
Free play. Flip, hop and count as you like.
Count again, one week or one month at a time.
You found each day by counting weeks and months.

observations.why: a week has seven days, so seven days after a date is the same day of the week.
observations.soWhat: hopping seven days at a time finds the same weekday again and again.
observations.observe: Every seventh date down one column lit in the same colour on the calendar page.

observations.why: the months take turns on the knuckles and in the dips, with February left alone.
observations.soWhat: the knuckle method gives the days of every month except February.
observations.observe: A card dropped on a knuckle read thirty-one and on a dip read thirty.

observations.why: an extra day is added to February every fourth year.
observations.soWhat: every fourth year is a leap year, with twenty-nine days in February and one more day in the year.
observations.observe: One February on the four-year strip grew a twenty-ninth square, once in four years.

observations.why: fifty-two weeks is three hundred and sixty-four days and a year has one day more.
observations.soWhat: a year is fifty-two weeks and one more day, not fifty-two weeks alone.
observations.observe: The week counter counted fifty-two weeks in a year and one day was left over.

source_tool.description: A real wall calendar page of 2026 hangs on a classroom wall at the left of the working area. It has a near-black top bar with the month and the year written large, a header row of the seven days of the week with Sunday first, and a grid of days in seven columns, the first of the month standing in its true column and the days of one week sharing a row. Two round buttons, an arrow left and an arrow right, flip the page like a leaf, and a pencil rests beside it. On the first phase a row of twelve small month cards lies beside the page, and tapping a row of the page counts its seven days. On the second phase two flat drawn fists stand beside the calendar, with their knuckles and dips labelled, and the child drops each month card on a knuckle or a dip, and the card reads thirty-one or thirty. On the third phase a four-year strip of four small wall calendars shows their Februaries side by side, and the leap year has a twenty-ninth square ringed in green; a year ruler from 1900 to 2099 in blocks of four lets the child step from one leap year to the next. On the fourth phase a pencil circles a date, a seven-day hop lights every seventh date down the same column in one colour, and a week counter counts the weeks between two circled dates. A number pad types a number of days, weeks, or a year, and a words box takes the name of a day. A Grid view button redraws the page as a plain table. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many days, weeks or months have been counted.
source_tool.art_direction: A classroom wall with a real calendar
