modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count again, one week or one month at a time.
voice.onNext: A new page. Find the day first.
voice.opening: A calendar on the wall, waiting to be flipped.
voice.onFinish: You found each day by counting weeks and months.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Flip, hop and count as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Days, weeks, months and a year
How many days in a month: the knuckle method
Leap year: every fourth year has 366 days
Finding a day and a date on a calendar

placement.where: After the class has looked at a real wall calendar together, found their own birthdays and said the knuckle months along their own fists, and before the leap year is named. The tool is what lets one February grow a twenty-ninth square on a four-year strip and what hops seven days down a column again and again, which a paper calendar cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: A week has seven days and a year has twelve months. A year is about fifty-two weeks and one more day, because fifty-two weeks is three hundred and sixty-four days and a year has three hundred and sixty-five. A month has twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty or thirty-one days. On the knuckles, a knuckle month has thirty-one days, a dip month has thirty days, and February has twenty-eight, or twenty-nine in a leap year. Every fourth year is a leap year, with twenty-nine days in February and three hundred and sixty-six days in the year. Adding seven days to a date gives the same day of the week, so the days between two dates are changed into weeks by counting in sevens, and a date a few days after a known day is found by counting on from that day.
answer_key.wrong: The calendar page is shown again with the dates counted along the column, a small number landing on each in turn, and the child's answer ringed on a second page beside it, so the two counts are seen side by side. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

steps: 1 week is 7 days.
4 weeks is 4 groups of 7 days.
4 times 7 is 28.
So the school trip lasts 28 days.
items.question: A school trip lasts 4 weeks. How many days is that?
items.checkpoint: A week has 7 days, so count the days in sevens.
items.misconception: Adding 4 and 7 to get 11 days instead of making 4 groups of 7 days.

steps: Say the months along the knuckles in turn: January is a knuckle, February is a dip, March is a knuckle, April is a dip, May is a knuckle, June is a dip, July is a knuckle.
So July is a knuckle month.
A knuckle month has 31 days, so July has 31 days.
items.answer: A knuckle month. July has 31 days.
items.question: A summer holiday lasts all through July. On the knuckles, is July a knuckle month or a dip month, and how many days does it have?
items.checkpoint: Knuckle months have 31 days and dip months have 30 days.
items.misconception: Calling July a dip month because it comes after June, which is a dip, and forgetting to count along the knuckles from January.

steps: A leap year comes every fourth year.
Count in fours from a leap year: 2040 is a leap year, and 2040 plus 4 is 2044.
So 2044 is a leap year.
In a leap year February has 29 days.
items.answer: 29 days, because 2044 is a leap year
items.question: A school wall calendar is printed for the year 2044. Does February have 28 or 29 days in that year?
items.checkpoint: Every fourth year is a leap year, and its February has an extra day.
items.misconception: Saying February always has 28 days, whatever the year.

steps: Count the days from 3 October to 31 October: 31 minus 3 is 28 days.
28 days is 4 weeks, because 4 times 7 is 28.
So the plant took 4 weeks.
items.question: A plant is put in a pot on 3 October 2026 and its first flower opens on 31 October 2026. How many weeks did the plant take?
items.checkpoint: Find how many days pass, then count them in sevens.
items.misconception: Counting 31 days and forgetting to take away the first 3 days.

items.question: A wall calendar has one page for each month of the year. How many pages does it have?
items.final_answer: 12 pages, one for each of the 12 months

items.question: A school term ends in June. On the knuckles, is June a knuckle month or a dip month, and how many days does it have?
items.final_answer: A dip month. June has 30 days.

items.question: A birthday card says 29 February. Which year has a 29 February, 2046 or 2048?
items.final_answer: 2048, because 2048 is a leap year and 2046 is not a leap year

items.question: A story book from the school library is borrowed on a Friday and is due in 2 weeks. On which day of the week is it due?
items.final_answer: Friday, because 2 weeks is 14 days and 14 days later is the same day of the week

items.question: A bus pass lasts one whole year. A year is 52 weeks and 1 more day. How many days does the pass last?
items.final_answer: 365 days, because 52 weeks is 364 days and 1 more day makes 365

items.question: A train runs every day through September and October. Which month has more days, and how many more?
items.final_answer: October has 1 more day. October is a knuckle month with 31 days and September is a dip month with 30 days.

items.question: A school notice says that last year was a leap year and that the next leap year will be 2048. What year is it now?
items.final_answer: 2045, because the leap year before 2048 is 2044, last year was 2044 and this year is 1 year later

items.question: Use the 2026 calendar. A school exam is on 24 June 2026, and 1 June 2026 is a Monday. On which day of the week is the exam?
items.final_answer: Wednesday, because 22 June is a Monday and 24 June is 2 days later

media.teaching_notes: Hang a real wall calendar in the room before the tool opens, and let the class find their own birthdays and the first day of the year. Say the knuckle months along fists together, and ask each child to count the days of one month for themselves. Fold a paper strip into four years and mark the leap year to show why one February is longer. Insist on counting the days between two dates by taking the first date away, and wait for a child to say why the same day comes back after seven days, rather than saying it for them. If a child says a year is exactly fifty-two weeks, ask how many days that is. Use fresh dates: the printed exercise asks about the calendar of the year, and the child's own answers come from the page in front of them.

topics.detailed_summary: The page shows the calendar of the year 2026 and says a year is twelve months or fifty-two weeks, a week is seven days and a month is thirty or thirty-one days or four weeks and a few extra days, except for February. The knuckle method counts the months on a fist: the months on the knuckles have thirty-one days, the months in the dips have thirty, and February has twenty-eight or twenty-nine. An example finds the third Sunday when the first of May is a Sunday, by adding seven days at a time, so it falls on the fifteenth. An ordinary year has three hundred and sixty-five days and February has twenty-eight, and after every fourth year February has twenty-nine and the year has three hundred and sixty-six, a leap year, because a year is really three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter of a day and four quarters make a whole day. An example finds the next three leap years after 2024, and another works out that exams from the first to the twenty-first of March last twenty-one days, which is three weeks. Exercise 10.3 continues with three questions this topic serves: seven questions on the calendar, finding the current year from the last leap year and the next leap year, and a Critical Thinking problem about a journey with a rest. The page then lists a Self-Assessment of four things the child can now do and eight vocabulary words, and the last page starts Apply Your Skills.

Add 7 each time to stay on the same day of the week. The 1st, 8th, 15th, 22nd and 29th are all Wednesdays. From 10 April to 24 April is 14 days, which is 2 weeks.

how_to_use.intro: Eleven numbered pages and a last page that opens on festival dates and closes on a honey eating race. The chapter names the two hands of a clock and reads the time to the minute, splits the day into a.m. and p.m., changes hours into minutes and days into hours, works out how long something takes and when it ends, writes a date in two ways, and reads a calendar and the leap year. Eight things on these pages need handling rather than copying. A year is 52 weeks and one more day, not 52 weeks. A year is only about 365 days and a quarter, so the leap year is taught as every fourth year. The Critical Thinking problem about the school bell needs the arrival time worked out first, so the bell rings ten minutes after it. The calendar questions use the printed calendar of 2026. The last leap year question needs the year before the next leap year. Noon and midnight never take a.m. or p.m. The opening box names festivals and the plan keeps to dates. The last page has no printed number and is filed as page 128.
points: Set a clock by hand before the tool is opened. A paper plate clock with two card hands is enough.
Say the minutes past or to the hour out loud every time a time is read, and say half past, quarter past and quarter to for the three special times.
Write a.m. and p.m. with the time, and never write them after noon or midnight.
Show an hour as sixty minutes and a day as twenty-four hours with real things: a clock face and a day strip.
To find how long, count from the start to noon and from noon to the end, then add.
Write a date in both ways and read it back to check that they say the same date.
Say a year is 52 weeks and one day, and that every fourth year has an extra day.
Leave the opening question with the child until dates have been written in both ways.

summary_stats.tool_note: Every tool is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode anywhere in this chapter, so each tool_config declares agent_control disabled rather than omitting it. Four Learn items and eight Practice items per tool, which is the primary-grade shape and not the Grade 6 to 10 one. Five tools at that shape carry 20 worked items and 40 practice items between them, one Learn item per phase and every phase represented in Practice.
summary_stats.counts_note: Five virtual tools, one per tool_id in the plan's own tool index, and one per teaching intention rather than one per printed exercise. Twenty tool phases across them, one per teaching concept of the topic each tool serves. One topic has no tool: the opener is a box about festival dates that asks how to write the dates of events, and the Concept Linking line that sends the child back to it is carried by the opener itself. One module, two segments, six topics and thirty-one concepts run over printed pages 117 to 127. Eight of the thirty-one are watch concepts, placed at the head of the tool topics, each holding its own video and driving no tool phase. They carry ten objectives, five real-life activities, nine videos and an image on each of the twenty-three teaching concepts, and the plan's time field works out at 3.4 across the six topics. recall_questions counts both topic level and segment level questions.

authoring_rules.flow: Topics follow the printed pages 117 to 127 in order. Every topic records the pages it comes from in source_page and source_pages. Nothing has been resequenced and nothing has been added.
authoring_rules.tools: Five virtual tools, all child-operated, built to the chapter's own interactive-tool contract: a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, pointer events only, no assets and no network. The governing rule is that the printed exercise is evidence, not structure, so there is one tool per teaching intention and not one per printed exercise. The chapter sets twenty-one exercises over eleven pages and a last page, counting the recap, the Critical Thinking boxes, the three numbered exercises, the bears and the Math Lab Activity, and they are five ideas: reading a clock, splitting the day into a.m. and p.m., changing hours and finding how long, writing a date, and reading a calendar. The question the opening box asks and the Concept Linking line that returns to it are carried by the opener itself. Worked examples are not registered, because an example is printed with its answer and asks the child nothing. Each tool names the printed exercises it serves, and the five lists together account for all twenty-one exercises exactly once.
authoring_rules.nesting: Module > segment > topic > concept. Media hang on a concept, never on a topic.
authoring_rules.concepts: Four teaching concepts on every topic that carries a tool, and three on the opener. A tool topic is headed by one or more watch concepts, each holding one video and driving no tool phase. The tool runs one phase per teaching concept, in the topic's order, and Learn walks all four. A concept on a tool topic is named with the phase it drives, as in When will it end? -Phase 4, while the phase itself carries the bare name. A real-life activity is not a concept: it hangs on the topic as the unplugged twin of that topic's tool.
authoring_rules.materials: A paper plate clock with two card hands, a real wall clock, a long paper strip for a day, a wall calendar, a stopwatch or a clock with a second hand for the teacher, and paper cards. Every tool assumes a time has been set, read or counted by hand first.
authoring_rules.questions: Four worked items and eight practice items per tool, worded for eight year olds. No scoring, no penalties, unlimited retries. Items use fresh numbers: no printed task's times, durations or dates appear with its operation or its answer, whether the task is an exercise, a worked example or a key line. Every conversion, end time, length of time and date in them was checked in exact arithmetic in Python, and every time statement is recomputed on every build. Noon and midnight never carry a.m. or p.m., and a clock time always carries a.m. or p.m. where the part of the day matters. A wrong answer is told in words, never written as a false equation, and no item is about prices or money.

source_textbook.note: Every topic carries the pages it was extracted from, and the pages run in order across the document. Each real-life activity names the printed span it is built from. The chapter is a twelve page scan with no text layer, read by eye: eleven numbered pages and a last page that carries no printed number, holding the questions of Apply Your Skills and the Math Lab Activity, filed as page 128. This chapter has no unit test. The chapter opens on page 117 straight after chapter 9's unit test. The opening page carries a competency tag line, C 3.2, C 4.1 and C 4.3, and a box about festival dates that asks how to write the dates of events like birthdays. A Concept Linking line on page 125 sends the child back to that box, and the opener carries both, because an opener has no tool. The chapter supplies its own objective register on page 127, a Self-Assessment of four can-dos: read the time in minutes on analog and digital clocks; tell when to write a.m. and p.m.; convert hours into minutes and days into hours; and read a calendar and write dates. The ten authored objectives map onto it, two to each of the five tools. Three printed passages are departed from. A year is said to be 12 months or 52 weeks, and 52 weeks is a day short of a year. A year is said to be 365 days and one fourth of a day, which is only about, so the leap year is taught as every fourth year. Question 3 of Exercise 10.3 says the current year while the printed calendar is 2026, so 2026 is used and named. Five more things are handled rather than copied, and the book is not wrong in any of them. The Critical Thinking problem about the school bell leaves the arrival time to be found before the bell, so the bell rings ten minutes after it. Question 4 of Exercise 10.3 needs last year to be the leap year, 2024, so this year is 2025. Noon and midnight take neither a.m. nor p.m. The festival names are not used. The last page is filed as above. The pages name people and animals, and no name of theirs appears anywhere in this plan.
source_textbook.title: Udgam School Mathematics, Grade 3

chapter_demands.principle: A clock is read by two hands that do two different jobs.
chapter_demands.explanation: The short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes. The minute hand moves five minutes from one number to the next and goes round once in sixty minutes. Set a real or a paper clock by hand before any time is read, and say the time out loud as minutes past or minutes to the hour.

chapter_demands.principle: A day is two turns of the clock, and a.m. and p.m. say which turn.
chapter_demands.explanation: The hour hand goes round twice in a day, so a day has twenty-four hours and the same clock face shows two different times of day. A.m. is from midnight to noon and p.m. is from noon to midnight, and noon and midnight take neither.

chapter_demands.principle: Hours and minutes change by multiplying, and how long is counted through noon.
chapter_demands.explanation: To change hours into minutes multiply by 60, and to change days into hours multiply by 24. To find how long something takes, count from the start to noon and from noon to the end, and to find when it ends add the time taken to the start.

chapter_demands.principle: A date and a calendar have their own rules.
chapter_demands.explanation: A date has a day, a month and a year and is written with the month in words or in numbers as DD-MM-YYYY. A week is seven days, a year is twelve months, a month has twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty or thirty-one days, and every fourth year is a leap year of three hundred and sixty-six days.

session_skeleton.note: Nothing should run longer than eight minutes without the child setting a clock, counting an hour or finding a date with their hands.
session_skeleton.intro: For a 25 to 30 minute session. The steps keep a real clock, a paper clock or a wall calendar in front of the child, because in this chapter every time and date is something that can be set, counted and pointed to.

steps.name: Retrieval
steps.description: Two quick questions answered before anything new. Which hand is the hour hand, and how many minutes make an hour?

steps.name: Do it by hand
steps.description: One clock setting, day strip or calendar task of the day's kind, done with a real or paper clock before anything is explained. Nothing is corrected yet.

steps.name: Name what you see
steps.description: The child says the time or the date aloud. Where the saying stalls is where the idea is missing.

steps.name: Teaching into the gap
steps.description: Short, and aimed at whatever the saying exposed.

steps.name: The tool
steps.description: The day's tool, Learn first and then Practice. The tool does what a real clock cannot do in front of the child: turn the hands through a whole day, lay a length of time along the clock, flip a calendar page.

steps.name: Check it
steps.description: The same answer checked another way: a time read again from the other side of the clock, a length of time counted back from the end, a date written in the other way.

steps.name: Say it aloud
steps.description: The answer said as a time with a.m. or p.m., or as a date, so the class hears one answer said two ways.

structural_points.explanation: A time may be said as 7:45 or as quarter to 8, and a date may be written in words or in numbers. Accept every correct way of saying the same time or date.

structural_points.principle: Say what the number is for.
structural_points.explanation: A number on a clock can be an hour or a number of minutes past or to. Ask which hand is meant, and which half of the day, before anything is read.
Noon and midnight take no a.m. or p.m. Write 12 noon and 12 midnight, and never 12 a.m. or 12 p.m.

virtual_tools_index.note: One tool per teaching intention, because the printed exercise is evidence and not structure. The chapter sets twenty-one printed exercises over eleven pages and a last page, and they are five ideas asked over and over with the help taken away a step at a time. The question the opening box asks and the Concept Linking line that returns to it are carried by the opener and are not in the register. Each of the five tools spans the exercises that share an intention and names them in its serves list, and those lists together account for all twenty-one exactly once. The bears of the last page are served by the converting tool, because they ask how long each bear took, and the Math Lab Activity by the same tool, because it finds how long one minute is. A phase's writeup describes the demonstration the builder sets up, and every tool's pad takes any number, so a worked item may set a different one in the same phase. Every tool is child-operated and runs one phase per teaching concept of its topic, and each does the part of its printed work that a real clock or calendar cannot. One turns the two hands of a wall clock and says each time as minutes past or to. One sweeps the hour hand twice round a day strip and sorts times into a.m. and p.m. One lays a length of time along a clock and a day strip, through noon, and changes hours and days. One builds a date in boxes and turns it from words into numbers and back. One flips the pages of a calendar, counts the knuckle months and finds a day. In every case a time is set, counted or pointed to by hand before the tool opens.

tools.pedagogical_advantage: Lets the child turn the two hands of a real wall clock and see the digital clock beside it change with them, which a printed clock shows only already set. The minutes can be written round the outer edge and the minute hand stepped from number to number, five minutes at a time, until twelve fives close a round of sixty minutes and the hour hand has crept on by the right amount. The right half of the face is tinted for minutes past and the left half for minutes to the next hour, so the side of the clock decides the words. A words card says each time aloud and in writing, and a time to draw is set by dragging the minute hand until the digital clock agrees. A plain dial is one tap away.

tools.pedagogical_advantage: Lets the child sweep the hour hand twice round a wall clock while a sun and a moon cross a day strip, which a printed pair of clocks cannot do, so twelve hours and twelve hours are seen to make a day of twenty-four. The strip is cut at noon in the middle and at midnight at both ends, with the morning half sky blue and the evening half amber, so a.m. and p.m. are two halves of one strip and not two words to learn. A picture card of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football, a dinner plate or a bed is dropped on its half, and a time card takes a time from the pad and a label from the a.m. and p.m. buttons, or the words noon and midnight, which take no label. A plain clock is one tap away.

tools.pedagogical_advantage: Lets the child see an hour fill with sixty minute marks, twelve fives at a time, and a day turn through twenty-four hour tiles, which a printed line of working only states. A length of time is a green bar laid along a day strip from its start to its end, and when the bar crosses noon it is drawn in two pieces that the child adds, so counting through noon is something that can be seen and not just said. Sliding the bar along the strip shows when a thing ends, and a column board takes the sums of hours and minutes with the carry shown. On the third phase six small clocks read as minutes after a start show a race where the longest and the shortest can be found at a glance. Every time is written the way it is said, with a.m. or p.m., and noon and midnight never carry either, which a page of loose sums cannot hold the child to.

tools.pedagogical_advantage: Lets the child build a date in a day box, a month box and a year box on a real card, and turn the very same date between the month in words and the month in numbers with one toggle, so two ways of writing are seen to name one date, which a printed pair of lines only states. A month ladder lists January to December with their numbers beside them, so the child finds that October is the tenth month by looking and not by counting on fingers. The boxes take two digits for the day and the month and four for the year, and a date that does not exist, such as the thirty-first of November, is refused in words with the reason, which a page of finished dates never shows.

tools.pedagogical_advantage: Lets the child flip a real wall calendar month by month and see that the days of a week are always the same seven columns, so the same weekday comes back every seven days, which a printed page shows only as one finished month. Two flat drawn fists carry the knuckle method, so the child drops each month card on a knuckle or a dip and sees thirty-one or thirty appear. A four-year strip of small calendars shows one February growing an extra square, so a leap year is seen to be every fourth year and not only said. A seven-day hop lights the same weekday down the column, and a week counter counts the weeks between two circled dates, which a pencil on paper does slowly and which no printed page can do twice. A plain grid view of the same page is one tap away.

Partners call out times such as quarter past six or ten minutes to three and set them on the plate. writeup.look: A wall clock with a vermilion hour hand and a deep blue minute hand, a digital clock beside it, a words card under them, the Minutes, Past and to and Plain dial buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Read the Clock' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many times have been read. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A plain wall fills the working area. The wall clock hangs at x 110, y 214, 400 across, drawn exactly: a cream face with a dark rim, twelve near-black numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand with no arrowheads, the hour hand creeping on as the minute hand turns. With the Minutes button on, the numbers 5, 10 and so on to 60 are written round the outer edge in deep blue. With the Past and to switch on, the right half of the face is tinted sky blue and labelled Past and the left half is tinted amber and labelled To. The digital clock hangs at x 560, y 214, 250 by 110, with its hours vermilion, its minutes deep blue and a near-black colon between them. The words card stands at x 560, y 360, 530 by 90, and says the time in writing, such as ten minutes past four. A green Answer tag at x 560, y 470, 260 by 70, holds the time the child has set or typed. In a task the clock sits in a small scene drawn behind it, a school hall, a bus stop, a railway station, a kitchen or a football ground. The Minutes button stands at x 110, y 650, 150 by 60, the Past and to switch at x 280, y 650, 190 by 60 and the Plain dial button at x 490, y 650, 160 by 60, each labelled in words. In the Plain dial view the same clock is drawn as a bare dial with its hands and no scene. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the hours and then the minutes of a time into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The clocks show the last time, with the words card saying it aloud and in writing and the digital clock beside the wall clock.

phases.win: the digital clock changes as each hand turns, and the hour and minute boxes light in their own colours
phases.does: drags each hand round, says which is which and what each tells, and watches the digital clock follow
phases.goal: the short hand is the hour hand and tells the hour, and the long hand is the minute hand and tells the minutes
phases.says: Two hands, two jobs. Which hand tells the hour?
phases.check: Away from the screen: the long hand of a clock is on the 12 and the short hand is on the 9. Which hand tells the hour, and what hour is it?
phases.feels: the two hands turning together and the digital clock following each one in its own colour
phases.hands: Make a paper plate clock with a short card hand and a long card hand, fix them with a split pin, and ask each child to point to the hour hand and then the minute hand.
phases.tries: First rung: point to the short hand and say its name. Second rung: move only the short hand and watch which box of the digital clock changes. Third rung: the same task with the long hand on the twelve, before it moves.

wrong.why: the longer hand seems the more important one
wrong.move: calls the long hand the hour hand because it looks bigger
wrong.screen: the digital clock changes its hours only when the short hand is moved, and the hours box lights vermilion while the long hand is moved and only the minutes box lights deep blue

wrong.why: the long hand is the easiest hand to see, so its number is read first
wrong.move: reads the number the long hand points to as the hour
wrong.screen: the hour box of the digital clock stays lit vermilion beside the short hand, and the words card says which hand each number belongs to

phases.screen: a wall clock in a school hall, a digital clock beside it, and the two hands waiting at the twelve
phases.soWhat: the short hand is the hour hand and tells the hour, and the long hand is the minute hand and tells the minutes
phases.concept: Two hands: the hour hand and the minute hand

phases.win: the hand closes a round, the hour hand has crept on a little, and a green tag reads one hour
phases.does: steps the minute hand from number to number counting in fives, then sends it once round the face
phases.goal: the minute hand takes five minutes from one number to the next, and twelve fives make a round of sixty minutes
phases.says: Move the minute hand one number at a time. Count in fives.
phases.check: Away from the screen: the minute hand moves from the 2 to the 6. How many minutes pass? Count in fives with your finger.
phases.feels: the minute hand stepping five minutes at a time until twelve fives close the round
phases.hands: Walk a finger round a paper plate clock from number to number, saying five, ten, fifteen, and write the minutes on the edge with a marker as you go.
phases.tries: First rung: count the numbers the hand passes. Second rung: count in fives as the hand is walked step by step. Third rung: the same task with one step only, before more steps are added.

wrong.why: the numbers are counted one, two, three, so each move feels like one
wrong.move: says one minute for each number the hand passes
wrong.screen: the minutes are written round the edge in deep blue, so the 3 carries 15, and the hand is walked again from the 12 with each step lit and counted in fives

wrong.why: the 12 is both the start and the end of the round
wrong.move: counts to the 11 and stops, so the round seems to end at the 11
wrong.screen: the hand is walked once more all the way round to the 12, which is written 60 as well as 0, and the round closes with a green tag that reads one hour

phases.screen: the wall clock with the minutes switched on round the edge and the minute hand standing on the twelve
phases.soWhat: the minute hand takes five minutes from one number to the next, and one round is sixty minutes
phases.concept: Five minutes from one number to the next

phases.win: the side lights up, the words card says the time, and the digital clock agrees
phases.does: sets the minute hand on a number, reads which side it is on, and says the time as minutes past or minutes to
phases.goal: on the right of the clock we say minutes past the hour, and on the left we count the minutes to the next hour
phases.says: Which side is the long hand on? Say minutes past or minutes to.
phases.check: Away from the screen: the long hand points to the 9 on a clock that is not at a special time. Is it on the left or the right? Do we say past or to?
phases.feels: the side of the clock choosing the word, past on the blue side and to on the amber side
phases.hands: On a paper plate clock, colour the right half sky blue and the left half amber, set the long hand on a number, and say whether it is on the blue side or the amber side.
phases.tries: First rung: say which side of the clock the long hand is on. Second rung: count in fives from the 12 on that side. Third rung: the same task with the long hand on the right side only, before the left side returns.

wrong.why: past is the first word a child learns for telling the time
wrong.move: says minutes past for a long hand on the left side
wrong.screen: the left half is tinted amber and labelled To, the minutes to the next hour are counted back from the 12 in deep blue, and the words card changes to minutes to

wrong.why: the number on the face is the first number seen
wrong.move: reads the minutes to the next hour as the number the long hand points to
wrong.screen: the minutes are counted in fives from the long hand round to the 12, each step lit amber in turn, and only that count is written on the words card

phases.screen: the wall clock at a bus stop with the right half tinted sky blue for past and the left half amber for to
phases.soWhat: on the right of the clock we say minutes past the hour, and on the left we count the minutes to the next hour
phases.concept: Minutes past and minutes to the hour

phases.win: the minute hand settles on its number, the words card says the time and the digital clock shows the same time
phases.does: reads a time with the long hand on the six, the three or the nine, then drags the minute hand to draw a time
phases.goal: the minute hand on the six is half past, on the three it is quarter past and on the nine it is quarter to the next hour
phases.says: Look at the long hand. Is it at the three, the six or the nine? Say the time.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a clock has its long hand on the 9 and its short hand just before the 5. Do we say quarter past or quarter to, and what hour comes next?
phases.feels: the long hand landing on the six, the three or the nine and the right words arriving with it
phases.hands: On a paper plate clock, put the long hand on the 6, the 3 and the 9 in turn, say the time each time, and then say a time aloud for a partner to set.
phases.tries: First rung: say which of the three marks the long hand is on. Second rung: say how much of the circle it has gone round. Third rung: the same task with the long hand on the 6 only, before the 3 and the 9 return.

wrong.why: half past is the first special time a child learns
wrong.move: says half past for a long hand on the 3
wrong.screen: the face lights the part of the circle the long hand has gone round, a half for the 6 and a quarter for the 3, and the words card changes to quarter past

wrong.why: the 9 is three quarters round, but the quarter word is the one remembered
wrong.move: says quarter past for a long hand on the 9
wrong.screen: the left half of the face is lit amber, only a quarter of the circle is left to go, and the words card says quarter to the next hour

phases.screen: a kitchen clock with three marks lit on the face and a time card waiting beside it
phases.soWhat: the minute hand on the 6 is half past, on the 3 it is quarter past, and on the 9 it is quarter to the next hour
phases.concept: Half past, quarter past and quarter to

writeup.delight: On the second phase, as the minute hand goes round a full circle, the hour hand creeps on so slowly that it seems to stand still, and when the round closes it has moved exactly one number, while a green tag lights up with one hour. On the fourth phase, the minute hand settles on the six and the whole right half of the face glows for a moment as the words card says half past.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a wall clock hangs in a school hall with both hands at the twelve and a digital clock beside it, and the words card is blank. On the second the minutes are written round the edge and the minute hand stands on the twelve, with a green tag waiting empty. On the third the clock hangs at a bus stop with its right half tinted sky blue and its left half amber, and the minute hand is already on a number. On the fourth a kitchen clock has three marks lit on its face, the three, the six and the nine, and a time card waits beside it. One thing moves, once: the minute hand gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any time on the wall clock, with the minutes round the edge, the past and to tint, the digital clock and the words card, and the plain dial one tap away. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the two hands and the digital clock, counting in fives, minutes past and to, the three special times and the rounds of the hands, each in a small real scene.
voiceLines: A wall clock and a digital clock, both waiting for the hands to move.
Two hands, two jobs. Which hand tells the hour?
Move the minute hand one number at a time. Count in fives.
Which side is the long hand on? Say minutes past or minutes to.
Look at the long hand. Is it at the three, the six or the nine? Say the time.
A new clock. Which hand will you read first?
Free play. Turn the hands and say the time as you like.
Look at the long hand again. Count the minutes in fives from the twelve.
You said every time by counting the minutes.

observations.why: the short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes.
observations.soWhat: the short hand is the hour hand and the long hand is the minute hand.
observations.observe: The digital clock changed when each hand was dragged, the hours when the short hand moved and the minutes when the long hand moved.

observations.why: one round of the minute hand is sixty minutes, which is one hour.
observations.soWhat: five minutes from one number to the next, and twelve fives make a round of an hour.
observations.observe: After the minute hand had gone once round, the hour hand stood one number further on.

observations.why: the right side counts minutes after the hour and the left side counts minutes before the next hour.
observations.soWhat: the side of the clock the long hand is on decides whether we say past or to.
observations.observe: A long hand on the right half gave the words minutes past, and on the left half gave minutes to the next hour.

observations.why: those three marks are halfway, a quarter and three quarters of the way round.
observations.soWhat: half past, quarter past and quarter to are the three special times to say.
observations.observe: The long hand on the six, the three and the nine gave half past, quarter past and quarter to.

source_tool.name: Read the Clock
source_tool.blurb: Turn the hands of a wall clock, count the minutes in fives, and say each time as minutes past or minutes to the hour.

serves.exercise: choosing the clock words that fill six blanks in the recap
writing the time shown on each of six school clocks
finding how many complete rounds each hand of a clock makes in a day and which makes more
writing the time in minutes past the hour and minutes to the next hour for three clocks
drawing the minute hand to show four given times

source_tool.description: A big wall clock hangs on a plain wall at the left of the working area, drawn exactly: a cream face with a dark rim, twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand, neither with an arrowhead, both dragged round by a finger. Beside it hangs a digital clock whose hours are vermilion and whose minutes are deep blue with a colon between them, and it changes as the hands turn. A Minutes button writes 5, 10 and so on round the outer edge of the face. A Past and to switch tints the right half of the face sky blue and the left half amber, labelled Past and To. A words card under the clocks says the time aloud and in writing, such as ten minutes past four. In the tasks the clock sits in a small scene, a school hall, a bus stop, a station, a kitchen or a football ground, and a green Answer tag holds the time the child has set or typed. The number pad types minutes and hours. A Plain dial button redraws the same clock as a bare dial. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many times have been read.
source_tool.art_direction: A school hall wall clock / Picture book

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the long hand again. Count the minutes in fives from the twelve.
voice.onNext: A new clock. Which hand will you read first?
voice.opening: A wall clock and a digital clock, both waiting for the hands to move.
voice.onFinish: You said every time by counting the minutes.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Turn the hands and say the time as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Two hands: the hour hand and the minute hand
Five minutes from one number to the next
Minutes past and minutes to the hour
Half past, quarter past and quarter to

placement.where: After each child has made a paper plate clock with two card hands and set a few times on it by hand, and before any time is written on the board. The tool is what lets both hands turn together while the digital clock follows, and what shows the hour hand creeping on as the minute hand goes round, which a paper clock turned by hand does not make easy to see.

answer_key.rule: A clock has two hands. The short hand is the hour hand and tells the hour. The long hand is the minute hand and tells the minutes. The minute hand takes 5 minutes to move from one number to the next, so counting in fives from the 12 gives the minutes past the hour. One round of the minute hand is 60 minutes, which is one hour. On the right side of the clock we say minutes past the hour. On the left side we count the minutes to the next hour. The minute hand on the 6 is half past, on the 3 it is quarter past, and on the 9 it is quarter to the next hour.
answer_key.wrong: The clock is shown again with its minutes written round the edge and the minute hand walked from the 12 to its number in fives, each step lit in turn, and the past and to tint shows which side it is on. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The short hand is the hour hand. It tells the hour.
The long hand is the minute hand. It tells the minutes.
The short hand points to the 2 and the long hand is on the 12, so it is 2 o'clock.
items.answer: The short hand is the hour hand. It is 2 o'clock.
items.question: The wall clock in the school library has its short hand pointing to the 2 and its long hand pointing to the 12. Which hand is the hour hand, and what hour is it?
items.checkpoint: The short hand is the hour hand and the long hand is the minute hand.
items.misconception: Calling the long hand the hour hand because it looks like the bigger hand.

steps: The minute hand takes 5 minutes to move from one number to the next.
From the 5 to the 6 is 5 minutes, from the 6 to the 7 is 5 more, and from the 7 to the 8 is 5 more.
Three moves of 5 minutes give 15 minutes.
items.question: The clock above the school bell has its minute hand on the 5. A little later the minute hand is on the 8. How many minutes have passed?
items.checkpoint: Each move from one number to the next is 5 minutes, so count in fives.
items.misconception: Saying 3 minutes, because the hand moved past 3 numbers.

steps: The long hand is on the right side of the clock, so we say minutes past the hour.
Count in fives from the 12: the 1 is 5 and the 2 is 10.
The short hand is just past the 4, so the hour is 4.
It is 10 minutes past 4, or 4:10.
items.question: At football practice the clock on the pavilion wall has its long hand on the 2 and its short hand just past the 4. How many minutes past the hour is it, and what time is that?
items.checkpoint: On the right side say minutes past the hour, and count in fives from the 12.
items.misconception: Saying 2 minutes past 4, because the long hand is on the 2.

steps: The long hand on the 6 is halfway round the clock.
Halfway round is half past the hour.
The short hand has passed the 2 and not reached the 3, so the hour is 2.
It is half past 2, or 2:30.
items.question: The kitchen clock has its long hand on the 6 and its short hand halfway between the 2 and the 3. What time is it? Say it with half past.
items.checkpoint: The minute hand on the 6 means half past.
items.misconception: Saying half past 3, because the short hand is near the 3.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: The digital alarm clock in the bedroom shows 5:20. Which number is the hour, and which is the minutes?
items.final_answer: The 5 is the hour and the 20 is the minutes

items.question: A kitchen clock has its minute hand on the 7. Count in fives from the 12. How many minutes past the hour is that?
items.final_answer: 35 minutes, counting 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35

items.question: The clock at the railway station has its long hand on the 8. Is the long hand on the left or the right side, and how many minutes is it to the next hour?
items.final_answer: The left side. It is 20 minutes to the next hour, because the 8 is 40 minutes past

items.question: A watch shows the long hand on the 3. Do we say quarter past or quarter to?
items.final_answer: Quarter past, because the long hand on the 3 is on the right and a quarter of the way round

items.question: At the bus stop a child says the long hand of the clock is the hour hand because it is longer. Is the child right? Which hand tells the hour?
items.final_answer: No. The long hand is the minute hand. The short hand is the hour hand and it tells the hour

items.question: The school bell rings when the long hand of the hall clock points to the 10 and the short hand is between the 2 and the 3. Say the time two ways.
items.final_answer: 10 minutes to 3, or 2:50

items.question: The alarm clock in the bedroom must ring at quarter to 5. Where does the minute hand point, and what is the time in numbers?
items.final_answer: The minute hand points to the 9. The time is 4:45

items.question: A clock in the school hall runs without stopping from midnight to noon. How many rounds does the minute hand make, and how many does the hour hand make?
items.final_answer: The minute hand makes 12 rounds and the hour hand makes 1 round, because from midnight to noon is 12 hours
