media_meta.generation_prompt: Build a clock-reading tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A big wall clock hangs at the left of the working area, drawn exactly: a cream face with a dark rim, twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand, neither with an arrowhead, both dragged round by a finger, the hour hand creeping on as the minute hand turns. A digital clock beside it shows the same time with the hours vermilion and the minutes deep blue. A Minutes button writes the minute numbers round the edge. A Past and to switch tints the right half of the face sky blue and the left half amber. A words card says the time aloud and in writing. A green Answer tag holds the time the child has set or typed. Each task sits in a small scene, a school hall, a bus stop, a station, a kitchen or a football ground. A Plain dial button redraws the clock as a bare dial. The number pad types hours and minutes. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of times read. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.

writeup.why: See that a day is two rounds of the hour hand and so has 24 hours, name 12 o'clock in the day noon and 12 o'clock at night midnight, and write a time with a.m. before noon and p.m. after it.
writeup.look: A day strip from midnight to midnight with a sky blue morning half and an amber evening half, a wall clock above it, a sun and a moon, picture cards, a time card with a.m. and p.m. buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Morning or Night' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many times have been placed on the day strip. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A day strip runs across the working area at x 90, y 420, 1000 by 120, from midnight at the left end to midnight at the right end with noon at its middle. The left half, from midnight to noon, is a sky blue band labelled a.m., and the right half, from noon to midnight, is an amber band labelled p.m. Near-black tick marks stand at the ends and the middle, labelled midnight, noon and midnight. A sunrise over a small school is painted at x 130, y 300, a high sun at the middle at x 560, y 290, and a moon over a street lamp at x 130, y 560 and again at x 1000, y 560. A wall clock hangs at x 90, y 210, 190 across, drawn exactly, with a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand and no arrowheads, and a Sun slider under the strip at x 320, y 600, 520 wide, carries a small sun along the strip while the hands of the clock turn with it, the hour hand going twice round from end to end. Picture cards, an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football, a dinner plate and a bed, each 90 across, wait at x 320, y 214 and are dragged onto the strip. The time card stands at x 330, y 650, 300 by 90, and takes a time from the pad. The a.m. button and the p.m. button stand at x 660, y 650 and x 780, y 650, each 100 by 60, and the Noon and midnight button at x 900, y 650, 190 by 60. A green Answer tag at x 840, y 214, 250 by 70, holds what the child has written. The Plain clock button stands at x 110, y 650, 160 by 60. In the plain view the wall clock is drawn as a bare dial. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the hours and then the minutes of a time into the time card. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The time card shows the last time written in full beside its picture, with the day strip lit on the half it belongs to.

phases.win: the second round ends, the day strip fills from end to end and a green tag reads one whole day
phases.does: turns the hour hand once round, then a second time, and counts the hours of each round
phases.goal: the hour hand goes round the clock twice in a day, twelve hours and twelve hours, so a day has twenty-four hours
phases.says: Turn the hour hand round the clock. How many times does it go round in a day?
phases.check: Away from the screen: the short hand of a clock has gone round three times. How many days have passed, and why not three?
phases.feels: the hour hand sweeping round twice while the sun crosses the whole strip
phases.hands: Hold up a real clock or a paper plate clock, turn the short hand all the way round twice, and count the hours of each round aloud, ending with the hours in all.
phases.tries: First rung: count the rounds of the hour hand aloud. Second rung: say how many hours one round is. Third rung: the same task with one round only, before the second round is added.

wrong.why: one round of the face is the only round a child sees
wrong.move: says a day has 12 hours because the clock face shows 12 numbers
wrong.screen: the hour hand is turned a second time while the sun is still crossing the strip, and the second round is counted in amber beside the first in vermilion until the strip is full

wrong.why: the sun looks as if it has done most of its work by the middle
wrong.move: counts only the hours of the first round and stops at noon
wrong.screen: the strip stays unfilled from the middle to the far end, a gap labelled Still to come, and the hand is turned on until the gap closes

phases.screen: a day strip from one midnight to the next with a wall clock above it and its hour hand waiting at the twelve
phases.soWhat: the hour hand goes round twice in a day, so a day has 24 hours
phases.concept: A day has twenty-four hours

phases.win: the middle of the strip lights as noon and the two ends light as midnight, with no label beside them
phases.does: slides the sun to the middle and to each end and names the twelve o'clock there noon or midnight
phases.goal: twelve o'clock in the day is noon and twelve o'clock at night is midnight, and neither takes a.m. or p.m.
phases.says: Both hands are at the twelve. Is the sun high, or is the moon out?
phases.check: Away from the screen: it is 12 o'clock and the street is dark and quiet. Is it noon or midnight, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the two twelves looking the same on the clock and different in the sky
phases.hands: Put a paper plate clock with both hands at the twelve beside two pictures, a bright sun and a dark night, and ask which picture goes with which twelve.
phases.tries: First rung: look at the sky and say if it is day or night. Second rung: say the word for 12 o'clock in the day and the word for 12 o'clock at night. Third rung: the same task with only the sun on the strip, before the moon returns.

wrong.why: both look the same on the clock face, so they get the same name
wrong.move: calls both twelves noon
wrong.screen: the sun is dragged to the end of the strip and the sky goes dark, the moon comes out over the street lamp, and the label changes to midnight

wrong.why: every time of a day has had a label so far, so noon seems to need one too
wrong.move: writes a.m. or p.m. after noon or midnight
wrong.screen: the label buttons grey out on noon and midnight, and the card reads noon or midnight alone with a small note that it stands alone

phases.screen: the day strip with a high sun over the middle and a moon over a street lamp at each end, and both hands at the twelve
phases.soWhat: 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight, and neither takes a.m. or p.m.
phases.concept: Noon and midnight

phases.win: the card settles in its half and the label a.m. or p.m. lights beside it
phases.does: drops a time or a picture card on the sky blue half or the amber half and says a.m. or p.m.
phases.goal: from midnight to noon is a.m. and from noon to midnight is p.m.
phases.says: Is it before noon or after noon? Drop it on its half.
phases.check: Away from the screen: you eat breakfast and you eat dinner. Which is a.m. and which is p.m., and where is noon between them?
phases.feels: the strip split at noon, the sky blue half on one side and the amber half on the other
phases.hands: Colour a long paper strip sky blue on the left half and amber on the right half, mark noon in the middle, and ask each child to stick a picture of their own day on it and say a.m. or p.m.
phases.tries: First rung: say whether the thing happens before or after noon. Second rung: drop the card on that half. Third rung: the same task with a time near the middle of the strip, before the times near the ends return.

wrong.why: the number looks small or big before the part of the day is thought about
wrong.move: chooses a.m. for any small number and p.m. for any big number
wrong.screen: the card is carried along the strip from midnight to its place, so the child sees which half it lands in, and the clock shows the same hour in both halves

wrong.why: lunch feels like part of the morning when the morning has been busy
wrong.move: puts a lunch box time on a.m. because lunch comes after the morning meal
wrong.screen: the strip is cut at the noon mark in the middle, and a lunch time is carried to the right of that mark and lands on the amber half

phases.screen: the day strip with its left half sky blue and its right half amber, and picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football and a dinner plate
phases.soWhat: from midnight to noon is a.m., and from noon to midnight is p.m.
phases.concept: a.m. and p.m.

phases.win: the time card is written in full beside the picture and the day strip lights the half it belongs to
phases.does: types the time for a picture card, chooses a.m. or p.m., or chooses noon or midnight, and reads it back
phases.goal: a time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, and noon and midnight are written as words with no label
phases.says: Type the time. Then choose a.m. or p.m., or noon or midnight.
phases.check: Away from the screen: say a time in the evening and write it with its label. Then say the same hour in the morning and write that too. How are they different?
phases.feels: the time card finishing only when a label or a word is chosen
phases.hands: Write the time of a favourite part of the day on a card, then write a.m. or p.m. after it, and swap cards with a partner to check.
phases.tries: First rung: say which half of the day the time is in. Second rung: choose the label for that half. Third rung: the same task with a time in the morning, before the evening return.

wrong.screen: the time card stays open with a small gap after the number and the strip lights both halves, asking which half, until a label is chosen

wrong.why: five seems a morning kind of number

wrong.screen: the card is carried along the strip and lands on the amber half, and the label p.m. lights beside it

phases.screen: the day strip with a picture card, a time card, the number pad, an a.m. button, a p.m. button and a Noon and midnight button
phases.soWhat: a time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, and noon and midnight are written as words
phases.concept: Writing a time with a.m. or p.m.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, as the Sun slider crosses the day, the hour hand sweeps round the wall clock and starts again at the twelve in the middle of the strip, and when the sun reaches the far end the sky changes from morning to evening light and then to a moon over the street lamp. On the second phase the sun settles at the middle of the strip with both hands at the twelve and the whole sky glows for a moment.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet placed. On the first phase the day strip is empty from midnight to midnight, the wall clock above it has both hands at the twelve, and a green tag waits empty. On the second a high sun stands over the middle of the strip and a moon over a street lamp stands at each end, with both hands at the twelve. On the third the left half is sky blue and the right half is amber, and picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football and a dinner plate wait beside the strip. On the fourth a picture card stands on the strip with a time card beside it, the number pad, an a.m. button, a p.m. button and a Noon and midnight button. One thing moves, once: the sun gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any time on the pad dropped on the strip, the sun slid from one end to the other, any picture card placed, and the a.m., p.m. and noon and midnight buttons. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the two rounds of a day, noon and midnight, a.m. and p.m., and writing a time in full, each in a small real scene.
voiceLines: A whole day on one strip, with a sun and a moon.
Turn the hour hand round the clock. How many times does it go round in a day?
Both hands are at the twelve. Is the sun high, or is the moon out?
Is it before noon or after noon? Drop it on its half.
Type the time. Then choose a.m. or p.m., or noon or midnight.
A new time. Find which half of the day it is in.
Free play. Slide the sun and place the times as you like.
Look at where the sun is. Is it before noon or after noon?
You put every time on the right half of the day.

observations.why: a day is two rounds of the hour hand, and the sun crosses the whole strip in a day.
observations.soWhat: a day has 24 hours, because 12 plus 12 is 24.
observations.observe: The hour hand went once round and the sun was only at noon, and it went round again before the sun reached the far end.

observations.why: both are 12 o'clock, one in the day and one at night, and each has its own word.
observations.soWhat: 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight, and neither takes a.m. or p.m.
observations.observe: The twelve of the middle was lit as noon and the twelve of the ends as midnight, and neither had a label.

observations.why: the strip is cut at noon, the sky blue half before it and the amber half after it.
observations.soWhat: from midnight to noon is a.m., and from noon to midnight is p.m.
observations.observe: A card dropped left of the middle took a.m. and a card dropped right of it took p.m.

observations.why: the same clock time falls once in each half of the day.
observations.soWhat: a time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, and noon and midnight are written as words.
observations.observe: A time typed on the card was not finished until a.m. or p.m. or a word was chosen.

source_tool.description: A long day strip fills the width of the working area, from midnight at the left to midnight at the right with noon in the middle. Its left half, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and labelled a.m., and its right half, from noon to midnight, is amber and labelled p.m. A sunrise over a school is painted at the left, a high sun at noon in the middle, and a moon over a street lamp at both ends. A wall clock hangs above the strip with a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand, and a Sun slider moves a sun along the strip while the hands turn with it, the hour hand sweeping twice round from one end to the other. Picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football, a dinner plate and a bed can be dragged onto the strip. A time card takes a time from the number pad and a label from the a.m. and p.m. buttons, and a Noon and midnight button writes the words noon and midnight, which take no label. A green Answer tag holds what the child has written. A Plain clock button redraws the clock as a bare dial. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many times have been placed.
source_tool.art_direction: A school day from sunrise to lamp light / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 3 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at where the sun is. Is it before noon or after noon?
voice.onNext: A new time. Find which half of the day it is in.
voice.opening: A whole day on one strip, with a sun and a moon.
voice.onFinish: You put every time on the right half of the day.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Slide the sun and place the times as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A day has twenty-four hours
Noon and midnight
a.m. and p.m.
Writing a time with a.m. or p.m.

placement.where: After each child has marked noon in the middle of a long paper strip, coloured the morning half sky blue and the evening half amber, and stuck picture cards of the day on it by hand. The tool is what sweeps the hour hand twice round while the sun crosses, and what puts a time and its label side by side, which a paper strip cannot do on its own.

answer_key.rule: A day has 24 hours, because the hour hand goes round the clock twice and 12 plus 12 is 24. 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight. The time from midnight to noon is a.m. The time from noon to midnight is p.m. A time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, but noon and midnight take neither.
answer_key.wrong: The day strip is shown again with the sun carried along it from midnight, the morning half lit sky blue and the evening half lit amber, and the time is dropped on the half it falls in. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Once round the clock is 12 hours.
Going round twice is 12 plus 12.
12 plus 12 gives 24, so 24 hours pass. That is one whole day.
items.answer: 24 hours, which is one whole day
items.question: The hour hand of the wall clock in the school hall goes once round the clock in 12 hours. How many hours pass while it goes round twice?
items.checkpoint: The hour hand goes round the clock twice in a day, so a day has 24 hours.
items.misconception: Saying 12 hours, because the clock face only shows 12 numbers.

steps: Both hands point to the 12, so it is 12 o'clock.
The sun is high in the sky, so it is the day.
12 o'clock in the day is noon.
items.answer: 12 noon, because the sun is high in the day
items.question: In the school kitchen the cook sees both hands of the wall clock pointing straight up to the 12 while the sun is high in the sky. Is it 12 noon or 12 midnight?
items.checkpoint: 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight.
items.misconception: Saying midnight because both hands point to the 12, without looking at the sun.

steps: Noon is the middle of the day.
From noon to midnight is p.m.
The evening is after noon, so 5:40 in the evening is 5:40 p.m.
items.question: The street lamp outside the school switches on at 5:40 in the evening. Is that a.m. or p.m.?
items.checkpoint: From midnight to noon is a.m. From noon to midnight is p.m.
items.misconception: Choosing a.m. because 5:40 looks like a small number.

steps: 6:55 in the morning is after midnight and before noon.
From midnight to noon is a.m.
So the time is written 6:55 a.m.
items.question: The alarm clock wakes a child for the school bus at 6:55 in the morning. Write the time with a.m. or p.m.
items.checkpoint: A time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it.
items.misconception: Leaving off a.m., so nobody can tell whether it is the morning or the evening.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.

items.question: The hour hand of the kitchen wall clock goes once round in 12 hours. How many times does it go round in a whole day?
items.final_answer: 2 times. A whole day has 24 hours

items.question: The moon shines over the street lamp and both hands of the clock point to the 12. Is this time called noon or midnight?
items.final_answer: Midnight, because it is 12 o'clock at night

items.question: Football practice starts at 3:45 in the afternoon. Is that a.m. or p.m.?
items.final_answer: p.m., because the afternoon is after noon. It is 3:45 p.m.

items.question: The class goes to the library at 9:25 in the morning. Write the time with a.m. or p.m.
A train leaves the station at one midnight and arrives at the next midnight. How many times does the hour hand of the station clock go round, and how many hours is that?
items.final_answer: Twice, and that is 24 hours

items.question: At noon the school lunch bell rings. A child writes noon as 12 and then adds p.m. What should be written instead?
items.final_answer: 12 noon. Noon takes no a.m. or p.m.

items.question: On a school day the sun rises at 6:20 in the morning, lunch is at 12:40 in the afternoon, football practice is at 4:50 in the afternoon and the child goes to bed at 10:15 at night. Which of these times are a.m. and which are p.m.?
items.final_answer: 6:20 is a.m. The times 12:40, 4:50 and 10:15 are p.m.

items.question: Write each time with a.m. or p.m., or write noon or midnight: the lamp at the school gate switches off at sunrise at 5:35 in the morning, the cook starts lunch at 11:45 before noon, the lunch bell rings at 12 o'clock in the day, and the night guard starts at 12 o'clock at night.
items.final_answer: 5:35 a.m., 11:45 a.m., 12 noon and 12 midnight

media_meta.generation_prompt: Build a day tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A long day strip fills the width of the working area, from midnight at the left to midnight at the right with noon in the middle. Its left half is sky blue and labelled a.m., and its right half is amber and labelled p.m. A sunrise over a school is painted at the left, a high sun at noon, and a moon over a street lamp at both ends. A wall clock hangs above the strip with a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand, drawn exactly, and a Sun slider moves a sun along the strip while the hands turn with it, the hour hand going twice round. Picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football, a dinner plate and a bed are dragged onto the strip. A time card takes a time from the number pad and a label from an a.m. button and a p.m. button, and a Noon and midnight button writes the words, which take no label. A green Answer tag holds what the child has written. A Plain clock button redraws the clock as a bare dial. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of times placed. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.

writeup.why: Change hours into minutes and days into hours with an hour filling and a day turning, find how long something takes by laying a bar along a day strip through noon, and find when something ends by sliding the bar.
writeup.look: A wall clock and a stopwatch at the left with a row of twelve five-minute tiles under them, a day strip of twenty-four hour tiles along the foot with a green bar laid on it, a column board, and on the third phase a row of six small clocks.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Time Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the minutes, hours or days now on the stage. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The real wall clock is 280 across at x 90, y 230, with its twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and its vermilion hour hand and deep blue minute hand, drawn exactly. The real stopwatch is a round brass face 130 across at x 400, y 240 with a start button on top. The row of twelve five-minute tiles runs at x 400, y 400, each tile 44 by 60 with a 6 gap, empty until the minute hand is dragged round, and labelled 5, 10 and on to 60 as it fills, with the words one hour at its end. The train ticket card or the calendar page card stands at x 690, y 232, 320 by 150, drawn as a real ticket or a real calendar page with its words and numbers. The day strip runs along the foot at x 90, y 610, twenty-four tiles each 40 by 50 with no gap, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m. and the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., with a notch and the words 12 noon between them and the words 12 midnight at both ends. The green bar is 40 tall at y 548, laid by dragging its two ends, and it is drawn in two pieces with their two lengths written above when it crosses noon. The column board stands at x 780, y 400, 240 by 150, an hours column and a minutes column with a carry slot above each. On the third phase six small clocks, each 100 across, stand in a row at x 90, y 240 in place of the wall clock, each with a tag that reads minutes after the start. On the fourth phase the flight card or the school bell card stands in the place of the ticket. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys, a colon key and two keys labelled a.m. and p.m., for typing a count of minutes, hours or days or a time with a.m. or p.m. into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The wall clock, the day strip and the bar show the last length of time or end time, with the hour in vermilion, the minutes in deep blue, the a.m. half sky blue, the p.m. half amber and the answer green.

phases.win: the twelfth tile fills, the row reads one hour, and the answer tag turns green
phases.does: drags the minute hand once round, watches the tiles fill to sixty, then types the minutes in the journey
phases.goal: one hour is sixty minutes, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by sixty
phases.says: One round of the minute hand fills an hour. How many minutes are in it?
phases.check: Away from the screen: turn a paper plate clock once round. How many minutes did the minute hand cover? Then turn it three times.
phases.feels: the minute hand sweeping round and the twelve tiles ticking full one after another
phases.hands: Time one minute with a stopwatch while the class claps, then turn a paper plate clock once round and say how many minutes that is.
phases.tries: First rung: how many minutes in one hour. Second rung: how many hours are in the journey, and how many minutes is each. Third rung: the same task with a journey of only whole hours, before the minutes come back.

wrong.why: the ticket writes two numbers side by side, so they seem to belong together
wrong.move: joins the hours and the minutes as one number
wrong.screen: the hours are changed on the clock first and the tiles fill that many hours, then the minutes are added in an amber tag after them

wrong.why: the minutes are already in the unit asked for, so they seem to be the whole answer
wrong.move: forgets to change the hours at all and gives the minutes alone
wrong.screen: the row of sixty tiles fills again once for each hour, and the count under it grows by sixty each time

phases.screen: the wall clock with its hands at twelve, an empty row of twelve five-minute tiles, and a train ticket card that shows a journey of hours and minutes
phases.soWhat: an hour is sixty minutes, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by sixty
phases.concept: Sixty minutes make an hour

phases.win: the last day's wheel settles, the count of tiles reads the hours, and the answer tag turns green
phases.does: turns the day wheel once to count the tiles, then turns it again for each day of the holiday and types the hours
phases.goal: one day is twenty-four hours, so days change into hours by multiplying by twenty-four
phases.says: The wheel turns once for one day. How many hours is that? Now for each day.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many hours are in one day? Then how many hours are in two days?
phases.feels: the day wheel turning once, each turn dropping twenty-four hour tiles into the count
phases.hands: Make a paper strip marked in twenty-four hours with noon in the middle, and count the tiles once for one day and again for each day of a holiday.
phases.tries: First rung: how many hours are on the wheel for one day. Second rung: how many turns of the wheel are in the holiday. Third rung: the same task with only two days, before the full holiday returns.

wrong.why: sixty was the number in the last phase, so it feels like the number for time
wrong.move: multiplies the days by sixty
wrong.screen: the wheel turns for one day and the tiles are counted aloud, one number for each, stopping at twenty-four

wrong.why: the wheel shows twelve sky blue tiles first, so twelve is the first number seen
wrong.move: multiplies the days by twelve
wrong.screen: the sky blue half and the amber half are both counted, and the two twelves are added on the wheel

phases.screen: the day wheel with its a.m. half sky blue and its p.m. half amber, noon notched, and a calendar page card that shows a holiday of some days
phases.soWhat: a day is twenty-four hours, so days change into hours by multiplying by twenty-four
phases.concept: Twenty-four hours make a day

phases.win: the bar splits at noon, its two pieces are added above it, and the total turns green
phases.does: drags the ends of the bar to the start and the end, watches it split at noon, adds the two pieces, and taps the longest and the shortest of the six clocks
phases.goal: the length of time between two times is found by counting to noon and from noon, and adding the two parts
phases.says: Lay the bar from the start to the end. Count to noon, then on from noon.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a class starts at ten in the morning and ends at one in the afternoon. How long is it up to noon, how long after, and how long in all?
phases.feels: a green bar laid along the day and splitting at the noon notch into two pieces that join into one total
phases.hands: Lay a strip of card along a day strip from a start to an end that crosses noon, cut it at noon, and add the two pieces.
phases.tries: First rung: where does the bar start and where does it end. Second rung: how long is the piece before noon. Third rung: the same task with an end before noon, so the bar does not split.

wrong.why: a smaller number minus a bigger one looks like the only sum on the page
wrong.move: takes the start time from the end time without passing noon
wrong.screen: the bar is laid along the strip from the start and is cut at the noon notch into two pieces, and the two pieces are counted aloud

wrong.why: the first piece is the one the finger lands on first
wrong.move: counts only the part before noon
wrong.screen: the second piece lights amber and its length is written above it, and the two lengths are added in a green tag

phases.screen: the day strip with a start and an end marked, a green bar waiting to be laid along it, a card that names a start and an end across noon, and the six small clocks of a race
phases.soWhat: to find how long something takes across noon, count to noon and from noon, and add the two parts
phases.concept: How long did it take?

phases.win: the bar's end lands on a tile, the end time reads on the strip, and the answer tag turns green
phases.does: slides the bar along the strip from the start, adds the hours and then the minutes on the board, and types the end time with a.m. or p.m.
phases.goal: the end time is the start time plus the time taken, hours first and then minutes, written with a.m. or p.m.
phases.says: Slide the bar from the start. Add the hours first. Then the minutes. Which side of noon is it?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a class starts at ten in the morning and lasts two hours. When does it end? What if it started at eleven and lasted two hours?
phases.feels: a green bar sliding along the day, over the noon notch, and stopping where the thing ends
phases.hands: Slide a strip of card along a day strip from a start time by the time taken, and read off where its end lands.
phases.tries: First rung: where does the bar start. Second rung: slide it by the hours only and say where it stops. Third rung: the same task with the time taken in whole hours, before the minutes come back.

wrong.why: the minutes are the smaller number and seem easiest to start with
wrong.move: adds the minutes first and loses the hours
wrong.screen: the bar slides along by the hours first and settles, then slides on by the minutes, so the two steps can be seen in turn

wrong.why: the start was a.m., so a.m. feels like part of the time
wrong.move: keeps a.m. after the end has passed noon
wrong.screen: the bar's end lands on an amber tile and the word p.m. is written there, with the noon notch lit as the bar crosses it

phases.screen: the day strip with a green bar of the time taken waiting at the start, a flight or a bell card that names a start and a length of time, and the column board
phases.soWhat: to find when something ends, add the time taken to the start time, hours first and then minutes, and say a.m. or p.m. by the side of noon
phases.concept: When will it end?

writeup.delight: Two small surprises. On the first phase, as the minute hand sweeps round, each five-minute tile fills with a small tick of the stopwatch and the last tile closes the row with the stopwatch button popping up. On the third and fourth phases, the green bar crosses noon and splits into two pieces that slide together into one total, and slid backwards they split again.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the wall clock stands with both hands at twelve, the row of twelve five-minute tiles is empty, and a train ticket card names a journey of some hours and minutes. On the second the day wheel stands with its sky blue half and its amber half and a calendar page card names a holiday of some days. On the third the day strip carries a start and an end across noon, a green bar waits beside it, and a row of six small clocks stands ready. On the fourth the green bar of the time taken waits at the start of the strip and a flight or a school bell card names the start. One thing moves, once: the minute hand, the wheel or the bar gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any count of hours, minutes or days on the clock and the wheel, the green bar slid along the day strip, and the column board. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on choosing minutes or hours, days into hours, a class that ends at noon, a lunch break, bottles filled in a minute, a night's sleep in a day, a school race on a stopwatch and when a school bell rings, each on a real thing.
voiceLines: A clock, a stopwatch and a day strip. Let us count the time.
One round of the minute hand fills an hour. How many minutes are in it?
The wheel turns once for one day. How many hours is that? Now for each day.
Lay the bar from the start to the end. Count to noon, then on from noon.
Slide the bar from the start. Add the hours first. Then the minutes. Which side of noon is it?
A new time to work out. What is it about?
Free play. Fill an hour, turn a day and slide the bar as you like.
Count again, one step at a time. Which side of noon are you on?
You counted the time with the hour filling and the day turning.

observations.why: the minute hand moves five minutes from one number to the next, and twelve fives make sixty.
observations.soWhat: an hour is sixty minutes, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by sixty.
observations.observe: One round of the minute hand filled twelve five-minute tiles and the row read sixty.

observations.why: the hour hand goes round twice in a day, once for the a.m. half and once for the p.m. half.
observations.soWhat: a day is twenty-four hours, so days change into hours by multiplying by twenty-four.
observations.observe: The day wheel turned once and counted twenty-four hour tiles, twelve sky blue and twelve amber.

observations.why: the day strip has a notch at noon, and the part before it and the part after it are counted apart.
observations.soWhat: to find how long something takes across noon, count to noon and from noon, and add.
observations.observe: A bar that crossed noon split into two pieces and the two lengths added up to the whole.

observations.why: the bar is as long as the time taken, so its end is the start plus that time.
observations.soWhat: to find when something ends, add the time taken to the start time, hours first and then minutes.
observations.observe: Sliding the bar from the start put its end on the time the thing finishes.

source_tool.description: A real wall clock, 280 across, stands at the left of the working area, with its twelve numbers, sixty minute marks and an hour hand and a minute hand, the hour hand vermilion and the minute hand deep blue. Beside it stands a real stopwatch with a round face and a start button. A row of twelve five-minute tiles runs under them, each tile 44 across. When the minute hand is dragged once round the clock the tiles fill one at a time, labelled 5, 10 and on to 60, until the row reads sixty minutes and a small label says one hour. Along the foot of the working area runs a day strip of twenty-four hour tiles, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m., the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., with a notch and the words 12 noon between them. A green bar the child sets by dragging its two ends is laid along the strip to show a length of time, and it is drawn in two pieces, with the two lengths written above them, when it crosses noon. Sliding the whole bar along the strip moves its end. A column board with an hours column and a minutes column takes a sum, with a carry shown above the column it joins. On the third phase a row of six small clocks, each reading a finishing time as minutes after a start, replaces the wall clock, and the child taps the longest and the shortest. A number pad sets any count and types any answer. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many minutes, hours or days are on the stage.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.

voice.opening: A clock, a stopwatch and a day strip. Let us count the time.
voice.onFinish: You counted the time with the hour filling and the day turning.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Fill an hour, turn a day and slide the bar as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Sixty minutes make an hour
Twenty-four hours make a day
How long did it take?
When will it end?

placement.where: After the class has timed one minute with a stopwatch, writing or clapping, and has sat a paper plate clock at the start and the end of a lesson. The tool is what fills an hour with sixty marks and lays a length of time along a whole day, which a paper plate cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so hours change into minutes by multiplying by 60, and an hour and some minutes is changed by changing the hours and adding the minutes. There are 24 hours in a day, so days change into hours by multiplying by 24. To find how long something takes, count from the start to noon and from noon to the end, and add the two parts; if it does not cross noon, count straight across. To find when something ends, add the time taken to the start time, hours first and then minutes, and write a.m. or p.m. by which side of noon the end falls on. Noon and midnight take neither a.m. nor p.m.
answer_key.wrong: The hour fills again slowly, one five-minute tile at a time, or the bar is laid along the day strip again and cut at noon into its two pieces, and the pieces are counted aloud. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: One hour is 60 minutes.
Change the hours first: 9 hours is 540 minutes.
Then add the 10 minutes. 540 plus 10 is 550.
So 9 hours 10 minutes is 550 minutes.
items.question: A train ticket shows a journey of 9 hours 10 minutes. How many minutes is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the hours into minutes first, then add the minutes.
items.misconception: Writing 910 by joining the 9 and the 10, or forgetting to change the hours at all.

steps: One day is 24 hours.
8 days is 8 times 24 hours.
8 times 24 is 192.
So 8 days is 192 hours.
items.question: A calendar page shows a holiday that lasts 8 days. How many hours is that?
items.checkpoint: A day has 24 hours, so multiply the days by 24.
items.misconception: Multiplying by 60, the minutes in an hour, because the last answer was done with 60.

steps: Count from 10 a.m. to 12 noon: 2 hours.
Then count from 12 noon to 3 p.m.: 3 hours.
Add the two parts: 2 plus 3 is 5.
So from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. is 5 hours.
items.question: A cricket match starts at 10 a.m. and ends at 3 p.m. How long does the match last?
items.checkpoint: Count to noon first, then on from noon, and add the two parts.
items.misconception: Taking 10 from 3, or counting 3 minus 10 as if the clock never passed noon.

steps: Add the hours first: 9:20 a.m. plus 3 hours is 12:20 p.m.
Then add the 45 minutes: 12:20 p.m. plus 45 minutes is 1:05 p.m.
The time passed noon, so it is p.m.
So the flight lands at 1:05 p.m.
items.question: A flight leaves at 9:20 a.m. and takes 3 hours 45 minutes. When does the flight land?
items.checkpoint: Add the hours first, then the minutes, and say a.m. or p.m. by which side of noon it is.
items.misconception: Writing 12:65 for the minutes, or keeping a.m. after the time has passed noon.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A child brushes teeth with a toothbrush and then sleeps in a bed all night. Which unit fits brushing teeth, minutes or hours? Which unit fits a night's sleep?
items.final_answer: Minutes fit brushing teeth, and hours fit a night's sleep

items.question: A bus tour on a calendar page lasts 10 days. How many hours is that?
items.final_answer: 240 hours, because 1 day is 24 hours and 10 times 24 is 240

items.question: A story class starts at 11 a.m. and ends at 12 noon. How long is the class?
items.final_answer: 1 hour, because from 11 a.m. to 12 noon is 1 hour

items.question: The school bell rings for lunch at 12 noon. Lunch lasts 1 hour. When does lunch end?
items.final_answer: 1 p.m., because 12 noon plus 1 hour is 1 p.m.

items.question: A child fills 3 bottles with a mug in 1 minute, timed on a stopwatch. How many bottles can the child fill in 1 hour at the same speed?
items.final_answer: 180 bottles, because 1 hour is 60 minutes and 3 times 60 is 180

items.question: A child sleeps in a bed for 9 hours each night. A day has 24 hours. How many hours of the day is the child awake?
items.final_answer: 15 hours, because 24 take away 9 is 15

items.question: Two children start a pot painting race at 12 noon and a stopwatch times them. The first stops at 12:25 p.m. and the second stops at 1:05 p.m. How much longer did the second child take?
items.final_answer: 40 minutes longer. From 12 noon to 12:25 p.m. is 25 minutes, and from 12 noon to 1:05 p.m. is 65 minutes

items.question: A child leaves home at 7:20 a.m. and takes 25 minutes to walk to school. The child reaches the gate 10 minutes before the school bell rings. When does the bell ring?
items.final_answer: 7:55 a.m., because 7:20 a.m. plus 25 minutes is 7:45 a.m., and the bell rings 10 minutes later

media_meta.generation_prompt: Build a time conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A real wall clock, 280 across, stands at the left of the working area with twelve numbers, sixty minute marks, a vermilion hour hand and a deep blue minute hand, and a real stopwatch stands beside it. A row of twelve five-minute tiles runs under them and fills one tile at a time as the minute hand is dragged once round, until it reads sixty minutes. A day strip of twenty-four hour tiles runs along the foot, the first twelve sky blue and labelled a.m., the next twelve amber and labelled p.m., noon notched between them. A green bar with two draggable ends is laid along the strip to show a length of time, and is drawn in two pieces with their two lengths written above them when it crosses noon, and the whole bar slides along the strip to show an end time. A column board with an hours column and a minutes column takes sums with the carry shown above the column it joins. On the third phase a row of six small clocks reading minutes after a start replaces the wall clock and the child taps the longest and the shortest. A number pad types counts and answers. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the minutes, hours or days on the stage. Noon and midnight never carry a.m. or p.m. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.

writeup.why: Say the day, the month and the year of a date, write a date with the month in words or in numbers as DD-MM-YYYY, and turn a date from one way into the other.
writeup.look: A real card with three rounded boxes for the day, the month and the year, a month ladder of twelve tiles with their numbers, a toggle between the month in words and in numbers, and a pad.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Write the Date' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many of the three boxes are filled. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The real card is a rounded card 560 by 300 at x 90, y 230, drawn as a birthday card, an invitation or a school notice in its natural colours with a line of words on it that names the event. The three rounded boxes stand in a row under the words at y 440: the day box 120 wide at x 130, the month box 220 wide at x 270 and the year box 160 wide at x 510, each 70 tall, with its label beneath in words, Day, Month and Year, so a part is told by its label before anything else. When the toggle is set to numbers, short dashes are drawn between the boxes. The month ladder is twelve tiles in two columns of six at x 740, y 232, each 150 by 54 with a 10 gap, each tile holding a month name and its number, January 01 down to December 12, and a tapped tile lights once. The month toggle is a button 300 by 64 at x 740, y 560 labelled Month in words and Month in numbers. A Check button stands under the card at x 90, y 580 (200 by 64), and a line in words under it says when a date is not a real one and why. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the day, the month number and the year into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last date in its boxes, written both ways, with the day, the month and the year each under its label and the month lit once on the ladder.

writeup.delight: Two small surprises. On the second and third phases, the month name or number lifts off its tile on the ladder and slides across into the month box. On the fourth phase, the toggle flips the whole date over like a page, and the three boxes keep the same day, month and year on the other side.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a real birthday card stands with its date written on it and three empty boxes under it, labelled Day, Month and Year. On the second a real invitation shows its three boxes filled in numbers, with the toggle set to the month in words. On the third a real school notice shows three empty boxes, the month ladder lit with its numbers, and the toggle set to the month in numbers. On the fourth a real diary page shows a date written in words at the left and an empty row of boxes at the right. One thing moves, once: the first box, or the toggle on the second and fourth phases, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any date the calendar allows in the three boxes, turned between the month in words and the month in numbers with the toggle, with the month ladder lighting each month. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.

voiceLines: A card with a date on it, and three empty boxes. Let us write it down.
A date has three parts. Which is the day? Which is the month? Which is the year?
Write the day first. Then spell the month out. Then the year. Read it aloud.
Find the month on the ladder. Its number goes in the middle. Two digits, two digits, four digits.
Say the date the other way. Turn the toggle. Do both ways name one day?
A new card. What is its day, its month and its year?
Free play. Write any date, and turn it between words and numbers.
Look at the labels under the boxes. Which part goes where?
You wrote the date in words and in numbers, and both said the same day.

observations.why: a date is made of three parts, and every part has its own place.
observations.soWhat: a date has a day, a month and a year, and all three are needed.
observations.observe: The day, the month and the year each had a box with a label under it.

observations.soWhat: Day-Month-Year writes the day, then the month in words, then the year.
observations.observe: The month name dropped into the middle box when it was tapped on the ladder.

observations.why: the number is the month's place in the year, and DD-MM-YYYY writes it with two digits.
observations.soWhat: DD-MM-YYYY writes two digits for the day, two for the month and four for the year.
observations.observe: The ladder showed a number beside every month, and the month box took two digits.

observations.why: the two ways write the same three parts, only the month is written differently.
observations.soWhat: a date in words and the same date in numbers name one date, so both are correct.
observations.observe: The toggle turned the date from words to numbers and the same day stayed on the card.

source_tool.description: A real card stands at the left of the working area, 560 by 300: a birthday card, an invitation or a school notice, drawn as a recognisable flat illustration in its natural colours with a line of words on it that names the event. Under its words sit three rounded boxes in a row, a day box 120 wide, a month box 220 wide and a year box 160 wide, each with its label beneath it, Day, Month and Year. A month ladder stands at the right, twelve small tiles in two columns of six, each tile 150 by 54 and holding a month name and its number, January 01 down to December 12. A toggle button labelled Month in words and Month in numbers turns the same date between the two ways of writing it: in the first the boxes read as in 7 November, and in the second they read as in 07-11, with the dashes drawn between the boxes. A pad types the day, the month number and the year. A short line in words under the card says when a date is not a real one, and why. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many boxes are filled.
